entries.85db45b6c052ccc16cf01a160cdeb810abcff187: <div sID="gen14185" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="20" osisID="Prov.20" sID="Prov.20"/> <div eID="gen14185" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd24770660049351640f63bfd6a30965379b5a56: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv57"/><title type="x-s3">Miscellaneous Maxims.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv57"/> <div sID="gen14186" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Wine <hi type="italic">is</hi> a mocker, strong drink <hi type="italic">is</hi> raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise. <div eID="gen14186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14187" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The mischief of drunkenness: <hi type="italic">Wine is a mocker; strong drink is raging.</hi> It is so to the sinner himself; it mocks him, makes a fool of him, promises him that satisfaction which it can never give him. It smiles upon him at first, but <hi type="italic">at the last it bites.</hi> In reflection upon it, it rages in his conscience. It is raging in the body, puts the humours into a ferment. <hi type="italic">When the wine is in the wit is out,</hi> and then the man, according as his natural temper is, either mocks like a fool or rages like a madman. Drunkenness, which pretends to be a sociable thing, renders men unfit for society, for it makes them abusive with their tongues and outrageous in their passions, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.29">ch. xxiii. 29</reference>. 2. The folly of drunkards is easily inferred thence. He that <hi type="italic">is deceived thereby,</hi> that suffers himself to be drawn into this sin when he is so plainly warned of the consequences of it, <hi type="italic">is not wise;</hi> he shows that he has no right sense or consideration of things; and not only so, but he renders himself incapable of getting wisdom; for it is a sin that infatuates and besots men, and takes away their heart. A drunkard is a fool, and a fool he is likely to be.
entries.4d777bbb5ba99671e70b9627d4ea4c52ec772376: <div eID="gen14187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14188" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> The fear of a king <hi type="italic">is</hi> as the roaring of a lion: <hi type="italic">whoso</hi> provoketh him to anger sinneth <hi type="italic">against</hi> his own soul. <div eID="gen14188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14189" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How formidable kings are, and what a terror they strike upon those they are angry with. Their <hi type="italic">fear,</hi> with which (especially when they are absolute and their will is a law) they keep their subjects in awe, <hi type="italic">is as the roaring of a lion,</hi> which is very dreadful to the creatures he preys upon, and makes them tremble so that they cannot escape from him. Those princes that rule by wisdom and love rule like God himself, and bear his image; but those that rule merely by terror, and with a high hand, do but rule like a lion in the forest, with a brutal power. <hi type="italic">Oderint, dum metuant</hi>—<hi type="italic">Let them hate, provided they fear.</hi> 2. How unwise therefore those are that quarrel with them, that are angry at them, and so <hi type="italic">provoke them to anger.</hi> They <hi type="italic">sin against their own lives.</hi> Much more do those do so that provoke the King of kings to anger. <hi type="italic">Nemo me impune lacesset</hi>—<hi type="italic">No one shall provoke me with impunity.</hi>
entries.986e833b1d23cc5e1a4162ac8d8c3ccb2d3636ca: <div eID="gen14189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14190" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> an honour for a man to cease from strife: but every fool will be meddling. <div eID="gen14190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14191" type="x-p"/> This is designed to rectify men's mistakes concerning strife. 1. Men think it is their wisdom to engage in quarrels; whereas it is the greatest folly that can be. He thinks himself a wise man that is quick in resenting affronts, that stands upon every nicety of honour and right, and will not abate an ace of either, that prescribes, and imposes, and gives law, to every body; but he that thus meddles is a fool, and creates a great deal of needless vexation to himself. 2. Men think, when they are engaged in quarrels, that it would be a shame to them to go back and let fall the weapon; whereas really <hi type="italic">it is an honour for a man to cease from strife,</hi> an honour to withdraw an action, to drop a controversy, to forgive an injury, and to be friends with those that we have fallen out with. It is the honour of a man, a wise man, a man of spirit, to show the command he has of himself by <hi type="italic">ceasing from strife,</hi> yielding, and stooping, and receding from his just demands, for peace-sake, as Abraham, the better man, <reference osisRef="Gen.13.8">Gen. xiii. 8</reference>.
entries.fe356bd01bf2cdfc6c4a413f9294e5a47d689773: <div eID="gen14191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14192" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> The sluggard will not plow by reason of the cold; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> shall he beg in harvest, and <hi type="italic">have</hi> nothing. <div eID="gen14192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14193" type="x-p"/> See here the evil of slothfulness and the love of ease. 1. It keeps men from the most necessary business, from ploughing and sowing when the season is: <hi type="italic">The sluggard</hi> has ground to occupy, and has ability for it; he can plough, but he <hi type="italic">will not;</hi> some excuse or other he has to shift it off, but the true reason is that it is <hi type="italic">cold</hi> weather. Though ploughing time is not in the depth of winter, it is in the borders of winter, when he thinks it too cold for him to be abroad. Those are scandalously sluggish who, in the way of their business, cannot find in their hearts to undergo so little toil as that of ploughing and so little hardship as that of a cold blast. Thus careless are many in the affairs of their souls; a trifling difficulty will frighten them from the most important duty; but good soldiers must endure hardness. 2. Thereby it deprives them of the most necessary supports: Those that <hi type="italic">will not plough</hi> in seed-time cannot expect to reap in harvest; and therefore they must beg their bread with astonishment when the diligent are bringing home their sheaves with joy. He that will not submit to the labour of ploughing must submit to the shame of begging. They <hi type="italic">shall beg in harvest, and</hi> yet <hi type="italic">have nothing;</hi> no, not then when there is great plenty. Though it may be charity to relieve sluggards, yet a man may, in justice, not relieve them; they deserve to be left to starve. Those that would not provide oil in their vessels begged when the bridegroom came, and were denied.
entries.890049a3f6ef1fa1ac09cf0f4850a353ae0ab5da: <div eID="gen14193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14194" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Counsel in the heart of man <hi type="italic">is like</hi> deep water; but a man of understanding will draw it out. <div eID="gen14194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14195" type="x-p"/> A man's wisdom is here said to be of use to him for the pumping of other people, and diving into them, 1. To get the knowledge of them. Though men's counsels and designs are ever so carefully concealed by them, so that they are as <hi type="italic">deep water</hi> which one cannot fathom, yet there are those who by sly insinuations, and questions that seem foreign, will get out of them both what they have done and what they intend to do. Those therefore who would keep counsel must not only put on resolution, but stand upon their guard. 2. To get knowledge by them. Some are very able and fit to give counsel, having an excellent faculty of cleaving a hair, hitting the joint of a difficulty, and advising pertinently, but they are modest, and reserved, and not communicative; they have a great deal in them, but it is loth to come out. In such a case <hi type="italic">a man of understanding will draw it out,</hi> as wine out of a vessel. We lose the benefit we might have by the conversation of wise men for want of the art of being inquisitive.
entries.67d929358efca4c5169f2c2b26cec6d0f386b84b: <div eID="gen14195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14196" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Most men will proclaim every one his own goodness: but a faithful man who can find? <div eID="gen14196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14197" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is easy to find those that will pretend to be kind and liberal. Many a man will call himself a man of mercy, will boast what good he has done and what good he designs to do, or, at least, what an affection he has to well-doing. Most men will talk a great deal of their charity, generosity, hospitality, and piety, will sound a trumpet to themselves, as the Pharisees, and what little goodness they have will proclaim it and make a mighty matter of it. 2. But it is hard to find those that really are kind and liberal, that have done and will do more than either they speak of or care to hear spoken of, that will be true friends in a strait; such a one as one may trust to is like a black swan.
entries.52c40b1ac4abf7a64b22205b4d1937288dd08ae1: <div eID="gen14197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14198" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> The just <hi type="italic">man</hi> walketh in his integrity: his children <hi type="italic">are</hi> blessed after him. <div eID="gen14198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14199" type="x-p"/> It is here observed to the honour of a good man, 1. That he does well for himself. He has a certain rule, which with an even steady hand he governs himself by: He <hi type="italic">walks in his integrity;</hi> he keeps good conscience, and he has the comfort of it, for <hi type="italic">it is his rejoicing.</hi> He is not liable to those uneasinesses, either in contriving what he shall do or reflecting on what he has done, which those are liable to that walk in deceit. 2. That he does well for his family: <hi type="italic">His children are blessed after him,</hi> and fare the better for his sake. God has mercy in store for the seed of the faithful.
entries.7503c173ddba0e3c247e5f3ed9860fe12dd42e87: <div eID="gen14199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14200" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> A king that sitteth in the throne of judgment scattereth away all evil with his eyes. <div eID="gen14200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14201" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The character of a good governor: He is <hi type="italic">a king</hi> that deserves to be called so who <hi type="italic">sits in the throne,</hi> not as a throne of honour, to take his ease, and take state upon him, and oblige men to keep their distance, but as a <hi type="italic">throne of judgment,</hi> that he may do justice, give redress to the injured and punish the injurious, who makes his business his delight and loves no pleasure comparably to it, who does not devolve the whole care and trouble upon others, but takes cognizance of affairs himself and sees with his own eyes as much as may be, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.9">1 Kings x. 9</reference>. 2. The happy effect of a good government. The presence of the prince goes far towards the putting of wickedness out of countenance; if he inspect his affairs himself, those that are employed under him will be kept in awe and restrained from doing wrong. If great men be good men, and will use their power as they may and ought, what good may they do and what evil may they prevent!
entries.56a8e29f2d6225cef75d18bb80518e1db7ec6d39: <div eID="gen14201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14202" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin? <div eID="gen14202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14203" type="x-p"/> This question is not only a challenge to any man in the world to prove himself sinless, whatever he pretends, but a lamentation of the corruption of mankind, even that which remains in the best. Alas! <hi type="italic">Who can say,</hi> "I am sinless?" Observe, 1. Who the persons are that are excluded from these pretensions—all, one as well as another. Here, in this imperfect state, no person whatsoever can pretend to be without sin. Adam could say so in innocency, and saints can say so in heaven, but none in this life. Those that think themselves as good as they should be cannot, nay, and those that are really good will not, dare not, say this. 2. What the pretension is that is excluded. We cannot say, We <hi type="italic">have made our hearts clean.</hi> Though we can say, through grace, "We are cleaner than we have been," yet we cannot say, "We are clean and pure from all remainders of sin." Or, though we are clean from the gross acts of sin, yet we cannot say, "Our hearts are clean." Or, though we are washed and cleansed, yet we cannot say, "We ourselves made our own hearts clean;" it was the work of the Spirit. Or, though we are pure from the sins of many others, yet we cannot say, "We are <hi type="italic">pure from our sin, the sin that easily besets us,</hi> the <hi type="italic">body of death</hi> which Paul complained of," <reference osisRef="Rom.7.24">Rom. vii. 24</reference>.
entries.bfb1a162d069bef9903ab24038beb8b4f309fd53: <div eID="gen14203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14204" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Divers weights, <hi type="italic">and</hi> divers measures, both of them <hi type="italic">are</hi> alike abomination to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen14204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14205" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. The various arts of deceiving that men have, all which evils the <hi type="italic">love of money</hi> is the root of. In paying and receiving money, which was then commonly done by the scale, they had <hi type="italic">divers weights,</hi> an under-weight for what they paid and an over-weight for what they received; in delivering out and taking in goods they had <hi type="italic">divers measures,</hi> a scanty measure to sell by and a large measure to buy by. This was done wrong with plot and contrivance, and under colour of doing right. Under these is included all manner of fraud and deceit in commerce and trade. 2. The displeasure of God against them. Whether they be about the money or the goods, in the buyer or in the seller, they are all <hi type="italic">alike an abomination to the Lord.</hi> He will not prosper the trade that is thus driven, nor bless what is thus got. He hates those that thus break the common faith by which justice is maintained, and will be <hi type="italic">the avenger of all such.</hi>
entries.7d755c3a04f917155fb4cccbc1546bce4974dc7e: <div eID="gen14205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14206" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Even a child is known by his doings, whether his work <hi type="italic">be</hi> pure, and whether <hi type="italic">it be</hi> right. <div eID="gen14206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14207" type="x-p"/> The tree is known by its fruits, a man <hi type="italic">by his doings,</hi> even a young tree by its first fruits, <hi type="italic">a child by his</hi> childish things, <hi type="italic">whether his work be clean</hi> only, appearing good (the word is used <reference osisRef="Prov.16.2">ch. xvi. 2</reference>), or <hi type="italic">whether it be right,</hi> that is, really good. This intimates, 1. That children will discover themselves. One may soon see what their temper is, and which way their inclination leads them, according as their constitution is. Children have not learned the art of dissembling and concealing their bent as grown people have. 2. That parents should observe their children, that they may discover their disposition and genius, and both manage and dispose of them accordingly, drive the nail that will go and draw out that which goes amiss. <hi type="italic">Wisdom is</hi> herein <hi type="italic">profitable to direct.</hi>
entries.614cb326d4ad18a7f18dacee664ce27cdcf5f527: <div eID="gen14207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14208" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> The hearing ear, and the seeing eye, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath made even both of them. <div eID="gen14208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14209" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. God is the God of nature, and all the powers and faculties of nature are derived from him and depend upon him, and therefore are to be employed for him. It was he that <hi type="italic">formed the eye</hi> and <hi type="italic">planted the ear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.9">Ps. xciv. 9</reference>), and the structure of both is admirable; and it is he that preserves to us the use of both; to his providence we owe it that our eyes are <hi type="italic">seeing eyes</hi> and our ears <hi type="italic">hearing ears.</hi> Hearing and seeing are the learning senses, and must particularly own God's goodness in them. 2. God is the God of grace. It is he that gives the ear that hears God's voice, the eye that sees his beauty, for it is he that opens the understanding.
entries.40428a50b03e1c6797384d3bb69a3824f9d2f8b5: <div eID="gen14209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14210" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Love not sleep, lest thou come to poverty; open thine eyes, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thou shalt be satisfied with bread. <div eID="gen14210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14211" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that indulge themselves in their ease may expect to want necessaries, which should have been gotten by honest labour. "Therefore, though thou must sleep (nature requires it), yet <hi type="italic">love not sleep,</hi> as those do that hate business. Love not sleep for its own sake, but only as it fits for further work. Love not much sleep, but rather grudge the time that is spent in it, and wish thou couldst live without it, that thou mightest always be employed in some good exercise." We must allow it to our bodies as men allow it to their servants, because they cannot help it and otherwise they shall have no good of them. Those that love sleep are likely to <hi type="italic">come to poverty,</hi> not only because they lose the time they spend in excess of sleep, but because they contract a listless careless disposition, and are still half asleep, never well awake. 2. Those that stir up themselves to their business may expect to have conveniences: "<hi type="italic">Open thy eyes,</hi> awake and shake off sleep, see how far in the day it is, how thy work wants thee, and how busy others are about thee! And, when thou art awake, look up, look to thy advantages, and do not let slip thy opportunities; apply thy mind closely to thy business and be in care about it. It is the easy condition of a great advantage: <hi type="italic">Open thy eyes and thou shalt be satisfied with bread;</hi> if thou dost not grow rich, yet though shalt have enough, and that is as good as a feast."
entries.ec011e1e8842488cd17f36c8c4ab517a8f17bf20: <div eID="gen14211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14212" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> naught, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> naught, saith the buyer: but when he is gone his way, then he boasteth. <div eID="gen14212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14213" type="x-p"/> See here 1. What arts men use to get a good bargain and to buy cheap. They not only cheapen carelessly, as if they had no need, no mind for the commodity, when perhaps they cannot go without it (there may be prudence in that), but they vilify and run down that which yet they know to be of value; they cry, "<hi type="italic">It is naught, it is naught;</hi> it has this and the other fault, or perhaps may have; it is not good of the sort; and it is too dear; we can have better and cheaper elsewhere, or have bought better and cheaper." This is the common way of dealing; and after all, it may be, they know the contrary of what they affirm; but the buyer, who may think he has no other way of being even with the seller, does as extravagantly commend his goods and justify the price he sets on them, and so there is a fault on both sides; whereas the bargain would be made every jot as well if both buyer and seller would be modest and speak as they think. 2. What pride and pleasure men take in a good bargain when they have got it, though therein they contradict themselves, and own they dissembled when they were driving the bargain. When the buyer has beaten down the seller, who was content to lower his price rather than lose a customer (as many poor tradesmen are forced to do—small profit is better than none), then he goes his way, and boasts what excellent goods he has got at his own price, and takes it as an affront and a reflection upon his judgment if any body disparages his bargain. Perhaps he knew the worth of the good better than the seller himself did and knows how to get a great deal by them. See how apt men are to be pleased with their gettings and proud of their tricks; whereas a fraud and a lie are what a man ought to be ashamed of, though he have gained ever so much by them.
entries.5a9dd396098372426f77c29617cc1327e9cacf51: <div eID="gen14213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14214" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> There is gold, and a multitude of rubies: but the lips of knowledge <hi type="italic">are</hi> a precious jewel. <div eID="gen14214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14215" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">lips of knowledge</hi> (a good understanding to guide the lips and a good elocution to diffuse the knowledge) are to be preferred far before gold, and pearl, and rubies; for, 1. They are more rare in themselves, more scarce and hard to be got. <hi type="italic">There is gold</hi> in many a man's pocket that has no grace in his heart. In Solomon's time there was plenty of gold (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.21">1 Kings x. 21</reference>) and <hi type="italic">abundance of rubies;</hi> every body wore them; they were to be bought in every town. But wisdom is a rare thing, a precious jewel; few have it so as to do good with it, nor is it to be purchased of the merchants. 2. They are more enriching to us and more adorning. They make us rich towards God, rich in good works, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.9-1Tim.2.10">1 Tim. ii. 9, 10</reference>. Most people are fond of gold, and a ruby or two will not serve, they must have a multitude of them, a cabinet of jewels; but he that has the lips of knowledge despises these, because he knows and possesses better things.
entries.3024bb7b336726a037b5643ed861f160dfae5ba5: <div eID="gen14215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14216" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Take his garment that is surety <hi type="italic">for</hi> a stranger: and take a pledge of him for a strange woman. <div eID="gen14216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14217" type="x-p"/> Two sorts of persons are here spoken of that are ruining their own estates, and will be beggars shortly, and therefore are not to be trusted with any good security:—1. Those that will be bound for any body that will ask them, that entangle themselves in rash suretiship to oblige their idle companions; they will break at last, nay, they cannot hold out long; these waste by wholesale. 2. Those that are in league with abandoned women, that treat them, and court them, and keep company with them. They will be beggars in a little time; never give them credit without good pledge. Strange women have strange ways of impoverishing men to enrich themselves.
entries.7b4763029930bfa3c9e611ac56d6f656a65a05c4: <div eID="gen14217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14218" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Bread of deceit <hi type="italic">is</hi> sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel. <div eID="gen14218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14219" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Sin may possibly be pleasant in the commission: <hi type="italic">Bread of deceit,</hi> wealth gotten by fraud, by lying and oppression, may be <hi type="italic">sweet to a man,</hi> and the more sweet for its being ill-gotten, such pleasure does the carnal mind take in the success of its wicked projects. All the pleasures and profits of sin are <hi type="italic">bread of deceit.</hi> They are stolen, for they are forbidden fruit; and they will deceive men, for they are not what they promise. For a time, however, they are <hi type="italic">rolled under the tongue as a sweet morsel,</hi> and the sinner blesses himself in them. But, 2. It will be bitter in reflection. Afterwards the sinner's <hi type="italic">mouth shall be filled with gravel.</hi> When his conscience is awakened, when he sees himself cheated, and becomes apprehensive of the wrath of God against him for his sin, how painful and uneasy then is the thought of it! The pleasures of sin are but for a season, and are succeeded with sorrow. Some nations have punished malefactors by mingling gravel with their bread.
entries.eab4cac40f53ed1604649fa1b7cfcf5ef2678311: <div eID="gen14219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14220" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> <hi type="italic">Every</hi> purpose is established by counsel: and with good advice make war. <div eID="gen14220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14221" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is good in every thing to act with deliberation, and to consult with ourselves at least, and, in matters of moment, with our friends, too, before we determine, but especially to ask counsel of God, and beg direction from him, and observe the guidance of this eye. This is the way to have both our minds and our purposes established, and to succeed well in our affairs; whereas what is done hastily and with precipitation is repented of at leisure. Take time, and you will have done the sooner. <hi type="italic">Deliberandum est diu, quod statuendum est semel</hi>—<hi type="italic">A final decision should be preceded by mature deliberation.</hi> 2. It is especially our wisdom to be cautious in making war. Consider, and take advice, whether the war should be begun or no, whether it be just, whether it be prudent, whether we be a match for the enemy, and able to carry it on when it is too late to retreat (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.31">Luke xiv. 31</reference>); and, when it is begun, consider how and by what arts it may be prosecuted, for management is as necessary as courage. Going to law is a kind of going to war, and therefore must be done with good advice, <reference osisRef="Prov.25.8">Prov. xxv. 8</reference>. The rule among the Romans was <hi type="italic">nec sequi bellum, nec fugere</hi>—<hi type="italic">neither to urge war nor yet to shun it.</hi>
entries.7dafeaeb0955f26737d85fb0466263ebcec7d103: <div eID="gen14221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14222" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> He that goeth about <hi type="italic">as</hi> a talebearer revealeth secrets: therefore meddle not with him that flattereth with his lips. <div eID="gen14222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14223" type="x-p"/> Two sorts of people are dangerous to be conversed with:—1. Tale-bearers, though they are commonly flatterers, and by fair speeches insinuate themselves into men's acquaintance. Those are unprincipled people that go about carrying stories, that make mischief among neighbours and relations, that sow in the minds of people jealousies of their governors, of their ministers, and of one another, that reveal secrets which they are entrusted with or which by unfair means they come to the knowledge of, under pretence of guessing at men's thoughts and intentions, tell that of them which is really false. "Be not familiar with such; do not give them the hearing when they tell their tales and reveal secrets, for you may be sure that they will betray your secrets too and tell tales of you." 2. Flatterers, for they are commonly tale-bearers. If a man fawn upon you, compliment and commend you, suspect him to have some design upon you, and stand upon your guard; he would pick that out of you which will serve him to make a story of to somebody else to your prejudice; therefore <hi type="italic">meddle not with him that flatters with his lips.</hi> Those too dearly love, and too dearly buy, their own praise, that will put confidence in a man and trust him with a secret or business because he flatters them.
entries.f05ebd2ae1456c63429355b5853d7b7d89169c9e: <div eID="gen14223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14224" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Whoso curseth his father or his mother, his lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness. <div eID="gen14224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14225" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. An undutiful child become very wicked by degrees. He began with despising his father and mother, slighting their instructions, disobeying their commands, and raging at their rebukes, but at length he arrives at such a pitch of impudence and impiety as to curse them, to give them scurrilous and opprobrious language, and to wish mischief to those that were instruments of his being and have taken so much care and pains about him, and this in defiance of God and his law, which had made this a capital crime (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.17">Exod. xxi. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.4">Matt. xv. 4</reference>), and in violation of all the bonds of duty, natural affection, and gratitude. 2. An undutiful child become very miserable at last: <hi type="italic">His lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness;</hi> all his honour shall be laid in the dust, and he shall for ever lose his reputation. Let him never expect any peace or comfort in his own mind, no, nor to prosper in this world. His days shall be shortened, and the lamp of his life extinguished, according to the reverse of the promise of the fifth commandment. His family shall be cut off and his posterity be a curse to him. And it will be his eternal ruin; the lamp of his happiness shall be <hi type="italic">put out in the blackness of darkness</hi> (so the word is), even that which is <hi type="italic">for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.13">Jude 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.13">Matt. xxii. 13</reference>.
entries.7cc59861021dd587b0a7ef6c196075dd89b4ad66: <div eID="gen14225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14226" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> An inheritance <hi type="italic">may be</hi> gotten hastily at the beginning; but the end thereof shall not be blessed. <div eID="gen14226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14227" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is possible that an estate may be suddenly raised. There are those that will be rich, by right or wrong, who make no conscience of what they say or do if they can but get money by it, who, when it is in their power, will cheat their own father, and who sordidly spare and hoard up what they get, grudging themselves and their families food convenient and thinking all lost but what they buy land with or put out to interest. By such ways as these a man may grow rich, may grow very rich, in a little time, at his first setting out. 2. An estate that is suddenly raised is often as suddenly ruined. It was raised hastily, but, not being raised honestly, it proves <hi type="italic">soon ripe and soon rotten: The end thereof shall not be blessed</hi> of God, and, if he do not bless it, it can neither be comfortable nor of any continuance; so that he who got it at the end will be a fool. He had better have taken time and built firmly.
entries.431dd6c9c95bf4e7fd9cfd4051c76d9e954d5b6a: <div eID="gen14227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14228" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Say not thou, I will recompense evil; <hi type="italic">but</hi> wait on the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and he shall save thee. <div eID="gen14228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14229" type="x-p"/> Those that live in this world must expect to have injuries done them, affronts given them, and trouble wrongfully created them, for we dwell among briers. Now here we are told what to do when we have wrong done us. 1. We must not avenge ourselves, no, nor so much as think of revenge, or design it: "<hi type="italic">Say not thou,</hi> no, not in thy heart, <hi type="italic">I will recompense evil</hi> for evil. Do not please thyself with the thought that some time or other thou shalt have an opportunity of being quits with him. Do not wish revenge, or hope for it, much less resolve upon it, no, not when the injury is fresh and the resentment of it most deep. Never say that thou wilt do a thing which thou canst not in faith pray to God to assist thee in, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou canst not do in mediating revenge." 2. We must refer ourselves to God, and leave it to him to plead our cause, to maintain our right, and reckon with those that do us wrong in such a way and manner as he thinks fit and in his own due time: "<hi type="italic">Wait on the Lord,</hi> and attend his pleasure, acquiesce in his will, and he does not say that he will punish him that has injured thee (instead of desiring that thou must forgive him and pray for him), but <hi type="italic">he will save thee,</hi> and that is enough. He will protect thee, so that thy passing by one injury shall not (as is commonly feared) expose thee to another; nay, he will recompense good to thee, to balance thy trouble and encourage thy patience," as David hoped, when Shimei cursed him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.12">2 Sam. xvi. 12</reference>.
entries.ba2ed4bab2f76cc152ccb4244c4372081b1b7176: <div eID="gen14229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14230" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> Divers weights <hi type="italic">are</hi> an abomination unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and a false balance <hi type="italic">is</hi> not good. <div eID="gen14230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14231" type="x-p"/> This is to the same purport with what was said <reference osisRef="Prov.20.20">v. 20</reference>. 1. It is here repeated, because it is a sin that God doubly hates (as lying, which is of the same nature with this sin, is mentioned twice among the seven things that God hates, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.17">ch. vi. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.19">19</reference>), and because it was probably a sin very much practised at that time in Israel, and therefore made light of as if there were no harm in it, under pretence that, being commonly used, there was no trading without it. 2. It is here added, <hi type="italic">A false balance is not good,</hi> to intimate that it is not only abominable to God, but unprofitable to the sinner himself; there is really no good to be got by it, no, not a good bargain, for a bargain made by fraud will prove a losing bargain in the end.
entries.1e23a3b791da35f4bfd1e8c036f33a58140ecf7b: <div eID="gen14231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14232" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Man's goings <hi type="italic">are</hi> of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; how can a man then understand his own way? <div eID="gen14232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14233" type="x-p"/> We are here taught that in all our affairs, 1. We have a necessary and constant dependence upon God. All our natural actions depend upon his providence, all our spiritual actions upon his grace. The best man is no better than God makes him; and every creature is that to us which it is the will of God that it should be. Our enterprises succeed, not as we desire and design, but as God directs and disposes. The goings even of a strong man (so the word signifies) <hi type="italic">are of the Lord,</hi> for his strength is weakness without God, nor is the battle always to the strong. 2. We have no foresight of future events, and therefore know not how to forecast for them: <hi type="italic">How can a man understand his own way?</hi> How can he tell what will befal him, since God's counsels concerning him are secret, and therefore how can he of himself contrive what to do without divine direction? We so little understand our own way that we know not what is good for ourselves, and therefore we must make a virtue of necessity, and commit our way unto the Lord, in whose hand it is, follow the guidance and submit to the disposal of Providence.
entries.eb2169ed843d74b7e71075120bd5dcbf8b2c40ee: <div eID="gen14233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14234" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> a snare to the man <hi type="italic">who</hi> devoureth <hi type="italic">that which is</hi> holy, and after vows to make enquiry. <div eID="gen14234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14235" type="x-p"/> Two things, by which God is greatly affronted, men are here said to be ensnared by, and entangled not only in guilt, but in trouble and ruin at length:—1. Sacrilege, men's alienating holy things and converting them to their own use, which is here called <hi type="italic">devouring</hi> them. What is devoted in any way to the service and honour of God, for the support of religion and divine worship or the relief of the poor, ought to be conscientiously preserved to the purposes designed; and those that directly or indirectly embezzle it, or defeat the purpose for which it was given, will have a great deal to answer for. <hi type="italic">Will a man rob God in tithes and offerings?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.3.8">Mal. iii. 8</reference>. Those that hurry over religious offices (their praying and preaching) and huddle them up in haste, as being impatient to get done, may be said to <hi type="italic">devour that which is holy.</hi> 2. Covenant-breaking. <hi type="italic">It is a snare to a man, after</hi> he has made <hi type="italic">vows</hi> to God, to <hi type="italic">enquire</hi> how he may evade them or get dispensed with, and to contrive excuses for the violating of them. If the matter of them was doubtful, and the expressions were ambiguous, that was his fault; he should have made them with more caution and consideration, for it will involve his conscience (if it be tender) in great perplexities, if he be to enquire concerning them afterwards (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.6">Eccl. v. 6</reference>); for, when we have opened our mouth to the Lord, it is too late to think of going back, <reference osisRef="Acts.5.4">Acts v. 4</reference>.
entries.caeed5e51047fc65da9d0b8935f9d0e0564e9c89: <div eID="gen14235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14236" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> A wise king scattereth the wicked, and bringeth the wheel over them. <div eID="gen14236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14237" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What is the business of magistrates. They are to be a terror to evil-doers. They must <hi type="italic">scatter the wicked,</hi> who are linked in confederacies to assist and embolden one another in doing mischief; and there is no doing this but by <hi type="italic">bringing the wheel over them,</hi> that is, putting the laws in execution against them, crushing their power and quashing their projects. Severity must sometimes be used to rid the country of those that are openly vicious and mischievous, debauched and debauching. 2. What is the qualification of magistrates, which is necessary in order to do this. They have need to be both pious and prudent, for it is the wise king, who is both religious and discreet, that is likely to effect the suppression of vice and reformation of manners.
entries.9a755ab8314f05c80ba8fd0803983125ecada456: <div eID="gen14237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14238" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> The spirit of man <hi type="italic">is</hi> the candle of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , searching all the inward parts of the belly. <div eID="gen14238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14239" type="x-p"/> We have here the dignity of the soul, the great soul of man, that light which lighteth every man. 1. It is a divine light; it is the <hi type="italic">candle of the Lord,</hi> a candle of his lighting, for it is <hi type="italic">the inspiration of the Almighty</hi> that <hi type="italic">gives us understanding.</hi> He <hi type="italic">forms the spirit of man within him.</hi> It is after the image of God that man is created in knowledge. Conscience, that noble faculty, is God's deputy in the soul; it is a candle not only lighted by him, but lighted for him. The Father of spirits is therefore called the <hi type="italic">Father of lights.</hi> 2. It is a discovering light. By the help of reason we come to know men, to judge of their characters, and dive into their designs; by the help of conscience we come to know ourselves. The spirit of a man has a self-consciousness (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.11">1 Cor. ii. 11</reference>); it searches into the dispositions and affections of the soul, praises what is good, condemns what is otherwise, and judges of the thoughts and intents of the heart. This is the office, this the power, of conscience, which we are therefore concerned to get rightly informed and to keep void of offence.
entries.7de9486a25c8b74bf513c540d3f197a5f403210e: <div eID="gen14239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14240" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> Mercy and truth preserve the king: and his throne is upholden by mercy. <div eID="gen14240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14241" type="x-p"/> Here we have, 1. The virtues of a good king. Those are <hi type="italic">mercy and truth,</hi> especially mercy, for that is mentioned twice here. He must be strictly faithful to his word, must be sincere, and abhor all dissimulation, must religiously discharge all the trusts reposed in him, must support and countenance truth. He must likewise rule with clemency, and by all acts of compassion gain the affections of his people. <hi type="italic">Mercy and truth</hi> are the glories of God's throne, and kings are called <hi type="italic">gods.</hi> 2. The advantages he gains thereby. These virtues will preserve his person and support his government, will make him easy and safe, beloved by his own people and feared by his enemies, if it be possible that he should have any.
entries.3c71a3375c0ea715e597f94ac71d4a238c66a6f8: <div eID="gen14241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14242" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> The glory of young men <hi type="italic">is</hi> their strength: and the beauty of old men <hi type="italic">is</hi> the gray head. <div eID="gen14242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14243" type="x-p"/> This shows that both young and old have their advantages, and therefore must each of them be, according to their capacities, serviceable to the public, and neither of them despise nor envy the other. 1. Let not old people despise the young, for they are strong and fit for action, able to go through business and break through difficulties, which the aged and weak cannot grapple with. The <hi type="italic">glory of young men is their strength,</hi> provided they use it well (in the service of God and their country, not of their lusts), and that they be not proud of it nor trust to it. 2. Let not young people despise the old, for they are grave, and fit for counsel, and, though they have not the strength that young men have, yet they have more wisdom and experience. <hi type="italic">Juniores ad labores, seniores ad honores</hi>—<hi type="italic">Labour is for the young, honour for the aged.</hi> God has put honour upon the old man; for his <hi type="italic">gray head</hi> is his beauty. See <reference osisRef="Dan.7.9">Dan. vii. 9</reference>.
entries.683f24f1d15130aec9f99f219c450c504d65c130: <div eID="gen14243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14244" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> The blueness of a wound cleanseth away evil: so <hi type="italic">do</hi> stripes the inward parts of the belly. <div eID="gen14244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14245" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Many need severe rebukes. Some children are so obstinate that their parents can do no good with them without sharp correction; some criminals must feel the rigour of the law and public justice; gentle methods will not work upon them; they must be beaten black and blue. And the wise God sees that his own children sometimes need very sharp afflictions. 2. Severe rebukes sometimes do a great deal of good, as corrosives contribute to the cure of a wound, eating out the proud flesh. The rod drives out even that foolishness which was bound up in the heart, and cleanses away the evil there. 3. Frequently those that most need severe rebukes can worse bear them. Such is the corruption of nature that men are as loth to be rebuked sharply for their sins as to be beaten till their bones ache. <hi type="italic">Correction is grievous to him that forsakes the way,</hi> and yet it is good for him, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.11">Heb. xii. 11</reference>.  <chapter eID="Prov.20"/> <div eID="gen14245" type="x-p"/>

entries.ac5313bf405388df63bb9525d5882b2b5e74469d: <div eID="gen24476" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen24477" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24478" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24478" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24477" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24479" type="x-p"/> Against wine and strong drink. We should avoid contentions. The sluggard. The righteous man. Weights and measures. Tale-bearers. The wicked son. The wise king. The glory of young men. The beauty of old men. The benefit of correction. <div eID="gen24479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24480" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen24480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24481" type="x-p"/> Wine is a mocker - It deceives by its fragrance, intoxicates by its strength, and renders the intoxicated ridiculous. <div eID="gen24481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24482" type="x-p"/> Strong drink - שכר shechar, any strong fermented liquor, whether of the vine, date, or palm species.
entries.407d83a58e60787c509ffc21d2c7fe14c930444d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen24482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24483" type="x-p"/> The fear of a king - Almost the same with <reference osisRef="Pro.19.12">Pro 19:12</reference> (note), which see.
entries.70169d0b639107acb07d3e93c5dfe1e3bc903bea: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen24483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24484" type="x-p"/> It is an honoer for a man - The same sentiment as <reference osisRef="Pro.19.11">Pro 19:11</reference>.
entries.b9fe96405a5a38ecd6bdc3837a6b74ebb440cb88: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen24484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24485" type="x-p"/> The sluggard will not plough - For other parts of this character, see the preceding chapter, Proverbs 19 (note). It is seldom that there is a season of very cold weather in Palestine; very cold days sometimes occur, with wind, rain, and sleet. They begin their ploughing in the latter end of September, and sow their early wheat by the middle of October. And this is often the case in England itself. The meaning of the proverb is: the slothful man, under the pretense of unfavorable weather, neglects cultivating his land till the proper time is elapsed.
entries.ea68fb375ed8df6cd8aaae5350e2c7ef32d630d0: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen24485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24486" type="x-p"/> Counsel in the heart of man - Men of the deepest and most comprehensive minds are rarely apt, unsolicited, to join in any discourse, in which they might appear even to the greatest advantage; but a man of understanding will elicit this, by questions framed for the purpose, and thus pump up the salubrious waters from the deep and capacious well. The metaphor is fine and expressive.
entries.132af8e31de15494749dda0a96314c21426098b8: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen24486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24487" type="x-p"/> Most men will proclaim - Many men merciful ben clepid: a feithful man forsoth, who schal finde? Old MS. Bible.
entries.35f36bc51cfb4bba00cbccdd6d7d97c3d085fcd4: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen24487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24488" type="x-p"/> A king that sitteth in the throne of judgment - Kings should see to the administration of the laws, as well as of the state transactions, of their kingdom. In the British constitution there is a court for the king, called the King's Bench, where he should sit, and where he is always supposed to be sitting. The eyes - the presence, of the monarch in such a place, scatter evil - he sees into the case himself, and gives right judgment, for he can have no self-interest. Corrupt judges, and falsifying counsellors, cannot stand before him; and the villain is too deeply struck with the majesty and state of the monarch, to face out iniquity before him.
entries.2c8c2ca0c07b88b3a000873c7a5c31d19bfaa891: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen24488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24489" type="x-p"/> Who can say, I have made any heart clean - No man. But thousands can testify that the blood of Jesus Christ has cleansed them from all unrighteousness. And he is pure from his sin, who is justified freely through the redemption that is in Jesus.
entries.33067a373762e5b2d441981e9cd841dc8e861c25: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen24489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24490" type="x-p"/> Divers weights and divers measures - A peise and a peise; - Old MS. Bible: from the French pois, weight. Hebrew: "A stone and a stone; an ephah and an ephah." One the standard, the other below it; one to buy with, the other to sell by.
entries.60c68cb7d2c0bca240e88c6410b4a2f71043a0f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen24490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24491" type="x-p"/> Even a child is known by his doings - That is, in general terms, the effect shows the nature of the cause. "A childe is known by his conversation," says Coverdale. A child is easily detected when he has done evil; he immediately begins to excuse and vindicate himself, and profess his innocence, almost before accusation takes place. Some think the words should be understood, every child will dissemble; this amounts nearly to the meaning given above, But probably the principal this intended by the wise man is, that we may easily learn from the child what the man will be. In general, they give indications of those trades and callings for which they are adapted by nature. And, on the whole, we cannot go by a surer guide in preparing our children for future life, than by observing their early propensities. The future engineer is seen in the little handicraftsman of two years old. Many children are crossed in these early propensities to a particular calling, to their great prejudice, and the loss of their parents, as they seldom settle at, or succeed in, the business to which they are tied, and to which nature has given them no tendency. These infantine predilections to particular callings, we should consider as indications of Divine Providence, and its calling of them to that work for which they are peculiarly fitted.
entries.fd718c72c5590634d0fc2063e8d2a6987c31ade4: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen24491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24492" type="x-p"/> The hearing ear and the seeing eye - Every good we possess comes from God; and we should neither use our eyes, nor our ears, nor any thing we possess, but in strict subserviency to his will.
entries.27f391e8690b75b89cbe2b26c893f7286ca9e284: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen24492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24493" type="x-p"/> Love not sleep, lest thou come to poverty - Sleep, indescribable in its nature, is an indescribable blessing; but how often is it turned into a curse! It is like food; a certain measure of it restores and invigorates exhausted nature; more than that oppresses and destroys life. A lover of sleep is a paltry, insignificant character.
entries.b981927d04baa28becba074c70d6c796cae2b06e: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen24493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24494" type="x-p"/> It is naught, it is naught, saith the buyer - How apt are men to decry the goods they wish to purchase, in order that they may get them at a cheaper rate; and, when they have made their bargain and carried it off, boast to others at how much less than its value they have obtained it! Are such honest men? Is such knavery actionable? Can such be punished only in another world? St. Augustine tells us a pleasant story on this subject: A certain mountebank published, in the full theater, that at the next entertainment he would show to every man present what was in his heart. The time came, and the concourse was immense; all waited, with deathlike silence, to hear what he would say to eaeh. He stood up, and in a single sentence redeemed his pledge: - <div eID="gen24494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24495" type="x-p"/> Vili vultis Emere, et Caro Vendere. <div eID="gen24495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24496" type="x-p"/> You all wish to Buy Cheap, and Sell Dear." <div eID="gen24496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24497" type="x-p"/> He was applauded; for every one felt it to be a description of his own heart, and was satisfied that all others were similar. "In quo dicto levissimi scenici omnes tamen conscientias invenerunt suas.' - De Trinitate, lib. xiii., c. 3; Oper. vol. vii., col. 930.
entries.ca87b2ce1d0a9d57f5388e53fe8608a74a4dab82: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen24497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24498" type="x-p"/> There is gold - Gold is valuable, silver is valuable, and so are jewels; but the teachings of sound knowledge are more valuable than all.
entries.b86e5c12f7b5452292d8271f71c9e7d11ddef35a: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen24498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24499" type="x-p"/> Take his garment that is surety for a stranger - I suppose the meaning to be, If a stranger or unknown person become surety in a case, greater caution should be used, and such security taken from this stranger as would prevent him from running away from his engagements.
entries.e633ef57b8826f2456e5c1a60023caba8722d216: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen24499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24500" type="x-p"/> Bread of deceit is sweet - Property acquired by falsehood, speculation, etc., without labor, is pleasant to the unprincipled, slothful man; but there is a curse in it, and the issue will prove it.
entries.ed1c8018d937061b458b5ec59a35e913a82219e7: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen24500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24501" type="x-p"/> With good advice make war, - Perhaps there is not a precept in this whole book so little regarded as this. Most of the wars that are undertaken are wars of injustice, ambition, aggrandizement, and caprice, which can have had no previous good counsel. A minister, who is perhaps neither a good nor a great man, counsels his king to make war; the cabinet must be brought into it, and a sufficient number out of the states of the kingdom gained over to support it. By and by, what was begun through caprice must be maintained through necessity. Places must be created, and offices must be filled with needy dependents, whose interest it may be to protract the war, till they get enough to pay their debts, and secure independence for life. And for these most important ends the blood of the country is spilled, and the treasures of the people exhausted! I have met with a fact precisely of this kind under the reign of Louis XIV.
entries.be23b43cc02c73534a12dba00ba8b5680ac98662: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen24501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24502" type="x-p"/> Whoso curseth his father - Such persons were put to death under the law; see <reference osisRef="Exo.21.17">Exo 21:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.20.9">Lev 20:9</reference>, and here it is said, Their lamp shall be put out - they shall have no posterity; God shall cut them off both root and branch.
entries.7f8d075f48cba422a2378985d23006cb6c0257b8: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen24502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24503" type="x-p"/> An inheritance - gotten hastily - Gotten by speculation; by lucky hits; not in the fair progressive way of traffic, in which money has its natural increase. All such inheritances are short-lived; God's blessing is not in them, because they are not the produce of industry; and they lead to idleness, pride, fraud and knavery. A speculation in trade is a pubiic nuisance and curse. How many honest men have been ruined by such!
entries.17a3852e55fa09692a371eaa6a809fff9d3675a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen24503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24504" type="x-p"/> I will recompense evil - Wait on the Lord; judgment is his, and his judgments are sure. In the mean time pray for the conversion of your enemy.
entries.da1a3805c58f20922077a294c8cd87f769767513: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen24504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24505" type="x-p"/> Man's goings are of the Lord - He, by his providence, governs all the great concerns of the world. Man often traverses these operations; but he does it to his own damage. An old writer quaintly says: "They who will carve for themselves shall cut their fingers."
entries.38943c33f629310216cdc6fece3a99a514de9bfa: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen24505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24506" type="x-p"/> Who devoureth that which is holy - It is a sin to take that which belongs to God, his worship, or his work, and devote it to one's own use. <div eID="gen24506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24507" type="x-p"/> And after vows to make inquiry - That is, if a man be inwardly making a rash vow, the fitness or unfitness, the necessity, expediency, and propriety of the thing should be first carefully considered. But how foolish to make the vow first, and afterwards to inquire whether it was right in the sight of God to do it! This equally condemns all rash and inconsiderate conduct. My old MS. Bible translates, Falling is of men often to vowen to seyntis, and after, the vouw is agen brawen. Is it possible that Wiclif could have translated this verse thus? as it strongly countenances vows to and invocations of saints.
entries.7190954923f6f8d10cc0fdefa3c943a43b1920c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen24507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24508" type="x-p"/> Bringeth the wheel over them - He threshes them in his anger, as the wheel does the grain on the threshing-floor. Every one knows that grain was separated from its husks, in Palestine, by the feet of the oxen trampling among the sheaves, or bringing a rough-shod wheel over them. Asiatic kings often threshed their people, to bring out their property; but this is not what is intended here.
entries.78d6da959e9c7aa9c2096c334d7e60a0c2f2edd5: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen24508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24509" type="x-p"/> The spirit of man is the candle of the Lord - God has given to every man a mind, which he so enlightens by his own Spirit, that the man knows how to distinguish good from evil; and conscience, which springs from this, searches the inmost recesses of the soul.
entries.49033fd84fcfd1f7c69e496fcb4db091f725770c: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen24509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24510" type="x-p"/> Mercy and truth preserve the king - These are the brightest jewels in the royal crown; and those kings who are most governed by them have the stablest government.
entries.f186312537698ca61ac15d032e1bcd99d1b17e76: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen24510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24511" type="x-p"/> The glory of young men is their strength - Scarcely any young man affects to be wise, learned, etc.; but all delight to show their strength and to be reputed strong. Agility, one evidence of strength, their particularly affect; and hence their various trials of strength and fleetness in public exercises. <div eID="gen24511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24512" type="x-p"/> And the beauty of old men is the gray head - They no longer affect strength and agility, but they affect wisdom, experience, prudent counsels, etc., and are fond of being reputed wise, and of having respect paid to their understanding and experience.
entries.bc7d6db1025a7884a191cd708685959436032d89: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen24512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24513" type="x-p"/> The blueness of a wound - חברות chabburoth, from חבר chabar, to unite, to join together. Does it not refer to the cicatrice of a wound when, in its healing, the two lips are brought topether? By this union the wound is healed; and by the previous discharge the lace-rated ends of fibres and blood-vessels are purged away. So stripes, though they hurt for the time, become the means of correcting and discharging the moral evil of the inmost soul, the vice of the heart, the easily-besetting sin. <div eID="gen24513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24514" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, verses fourteen to nineteen, inclusive, are wanting in the Septuagint and Arabic; and the tenth, eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth, come in after the twenty-second. It is difficult to account for these variations, unless they were occasioned by the change of leaves in MSS.  <chapter eID="Prov.20"/> <div eID="gen24514" type="x-p"/>

entries.8bbc6e334042910f79522b41c83d2b31b4218c7f: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.1">Pro 20:1</reference> <div eID="gen11393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11394" type="x-p"/> This proverb warns against the debauchery with which free-thinking is intimately associated. <div eID="gen11394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11395" type="x-p"/> Wine is a mocker, mead boisterous; <div eID="gen11395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11396" type="x-p"/> And no one who is overtaken thereby is wise. <div eID="gen11396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11397" type="x-p"/> The article stands with יין. Ewald maintains that in 10:1-22:6 the article occurs only here and at <reference osisRef="Prov.21.31">Pro 21:31</reference>, and that it is here, as the lxx shows, not original. Both statements are incorrect. The article is found, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Prov.19.6">Pro 19:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.18.18">Pro 18:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.17">Pro 18:17</reference>, and here the personification of “wine” requires it; but that it is wanting to שׁכר shows how little poetry delights in it; it stands once for twice. The effects of wine and mead (שׁכר from שׁכר, to stop, obstruct, become stupid) are attributed to these liquors themselves as their property. Wine is a mocker, because he who is intoxicated with it readily scoffs at that which is holy; mead is boisterous (cf. הומיּה, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.11">Pro 7:11</reference>), because he who is inebriated in his dissolute madness breaks through the limits of morality and propriety. He is unwise who, through wine and the like, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, overpowered by it (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.13.28">2Sa 13:28</reference>), staggers, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, he gives himself up to wine to such a degree that he is no longer master of himself. At <reference osisRef="Prov.5.19">Pro 5:19</reference> we read, שׁגה ב, of the intoxication of love; here, as at <reference osisRef="Isa.28.7">Isa 28:7</reference>, of the intoxication of wine, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of the passionate slavish desire of wine or for wine. The word “<hi type="italic">Erpicht</hi>” [<hi type="italic">avidissimus</hi>], <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, being indissolubly bound to a thing, corresponds at least in some degree to the idea. Fleischer compares the French: <hi type="italic">être fou de quelque chose</hi>. <reference osisRef="Isa.28.7">Isa 28:7</reference>, however, shows that one has to think on actual staggering, being overtaken in wine.
entries.ff223e672719bee9d57ee57fc6baee51e4a722f4: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.2">Pro 20:2</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.2">2</reference> A roaring as of a lion is the terror of the king;    And he that provoketh him forfeiteth his life. <div eID="gen11397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11398" type="x-p"/> Line first is a variation of Pro 19:12. The terror which a king spreads around (מלך, <hi type="italic">gen. subjecti</hi>., as, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Job.9.34">Job 9:34</reference> and generally) is like the growling of a lion which threatens danger. The thought here suggested is that it is dangerous to arouse a lion. Thus מתעבּרו does not mean: he who is angry at him (<hi type="italic">Venet</hi>.: χολούμενος αὐτῷ), but he who provokes him (lxx, Syr., Targ., Jerome, Luther). התעבּר signifies, as we saw at <reference osisRef="Prov.14.16">Pro 14:16</reference>, to be in a state of excessive displeasure, extreme anger. Here the meaning must be: he who puts him into a state of anger (lxx, ὁ παροξύνων αὐτόν, in other versions with the addition of καὶ ἐπιμιγνύμενος, who conducts himself familiarly towards him = מתערבו). But can mitharvo have this meaning? That the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. of transitive stems, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, התחגּן (1Ki 8:59) and השׁתּמּר (Mic 6:16), is construed with the accus. of that which any one performs for himself (cf. Ewald’s <hi type="italic">Gramm. Arab</hi>. §180), is not unusual; but can the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. of the intrans. עבר, which signifies to fall into a passion, “express with the accusative the passion of another excited thereby” (Ewald, §282a)? There is no evidence for this; and Hitzig’s conjecture, מתעבּרו (<hi type="italic">Tiphel</hi> of the Targ. תּעבור = עברה), is thus not without occasion. But one might suppose that התעבּר, as the reflexive of a <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> or <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> which meant to be put into a state of anger, may mean to draw forth the anger of any one, as in Arab., the VIIIth form (<hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>.) of ḥaḍr, to be present, with the accus. as reflexive of the IVth form, may mean: <hi type="italic">sibi aliquid praesens sistere</hi>. Not so difficult is חטא with the accus. of that which is missing, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.8.36">Pro 8:36</reference> and Hab 2:10.
entries.68ceda030b6e41a0faebbc9562fbac37b434da64: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.3">Pro 20:3</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.3">3</reference> It is an honour to a man to remain far from strife;    But every fool showeth his teeth. <div eID="gen11398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11399" type="x-p"/> Or better: whoever is a fool <hi type="italic">quisquis amens</hi>, for the emphasis does not lie on this, that every fool, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, every single one of this sort, contends to the uttermost; but that whoever is only always a fool finds pleasure in such strife. Regarding התגּלּע, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.17.14">Pro 17:14</reference>; Pro 18:1. On the contrary, it is an honour to a man to be peaceable, or, as it is here expressed, to remain far from strife. The phrase may be translated: to desist from strife; but in this case the word would be pointed שׁבת, which Hitzig prefers; for שׁבת from שׁבת means, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.7">2Sa 23:7</reference>, annihilation (the termination of existence); also <reference osisRef="Exod.21.19">Exo 21:19</reference>, שׁבתּו does not mean to be keeping holy day; but to be sitting, viz., at home, in a state of incapability for work. Rightly Fleischer: “ישׁב מן, like Arab. ḳ'ad ṣan, to remain sitting quiet, and thus to hold oneself removed from any kind of activity.” He who is prudent, and cares for his honour, not only breaks off strife when it threatens to become passionate, but does not at all enter into it, keeps himself far removed from it.
entries.fe29b3fa1a701006745bc6ea04abe05258a75fc5: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.4">Pro 20:4</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.4">4</reference> At the beginning of the harvest the sluggard plougheth not;    And so when he cometh to the reaping-time there is nothing. <div eID="gen11399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11400" type="x-p"/> Many translators (Symmachus, Jerome, Luther) and interpreters (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Rashi, Zöckler) explain: <hi type="italic">propter frigus</hi>; but חרף is, according to its verbal import, not a synon. of קר and צנּה, but means gathering = the time of gathering (synon. אסיף), from חרף, <hi type="italic">carpere</hi>,<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Fleischer in Levy’s <hi type="italic">Chald. Wörterbuch</hi>, i. 426.</note> as harvest, the time of the καρπίζειν, the plucking off of the fruit; but the harvest is the beginning of the old Eastern agricultural year, for in Palestine and Syria the time of ploughing and sowing with the harvest or early rains (חריף = יורה, <reference osisRef="Neh.7.24">Neh 7:24</reference>; Ezr 2:18) followed the fruit harvest from October to December. The מן is thus not that of cause but of time. Thus rendered, it may mean the beginning of an event and onwards (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.25">1Sa 30:25</reference>), as well as its termination and onwards (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.17">Lev 27:17</reference>): here of the harvest and its ingathering and onwards. In 4b, the Chethı̂b and Kerı̂ vary as at Pro 18:17. The <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. ישׁאל would denote what stands before the sluggard; the perf. שׁאלו places him in the midst of this, and besides has this in its favour, that, interpreted as <hi type="italic">perf. hypotheticum</hi>, it makes the absence of an object to שׁאל more tenable. The Chethı̂b, ושׁאל, is not to be read after <reference osisRef="Ps.109.10">Psa 109:10</reference> : he will beg in harvest - in vain (Jerome, Luther), to which Hitzig well remarks: Why in vain? Amid the joy of harvest people dispense most liberally; and the right time for begging comes later. Hitzig conjecturally arrives at the translation: “A pannier the sluggard provideth not; <div eID="gen11400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11401" type="x-p"/> Seeketh to borrow in harvest, and nothing cometh of it.” <div eID="gen11401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11402" type="x-p"/> But leaving out of view the “pannier,” the meaning “to obtain something as a loan,” which שׁאל from the connection may bear, is here altogether imaginary. Let one imagine to himself an indolent owner of land, who does not trouble himself about the filling and sowing of his fields at the right time and with diligence, but leaves this to his people, who do only as much as is commanded them: such an one asks, when now the harvest-time has come, about the ingathering; but he receives the answer, that the land has lain unploughed, because he had not commanded it to be ploughed. When he asks, there is nothing, he asks in vain (ואין, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.14.6">Pro 14:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.13.4">Pro 13:4</reference>). Meîri rightly explains מחרף by מתחלת זמן החרישׁה, and 4b by: “so then, when he asks at harvest time, he will find nothing;” on the other hand, the lxx and Aram. think on חרף, <hi type="italic">carpere conviciis</hi>, as also in Codd. here and there is found the meaningless מחרף.
entries.d1cb150e9e7621ba4340f266773e64fe000bffd5: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.5">Pro 20:5</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.5">5</reference> The purpose in the heart of a man is deep water;    But a man of understanding draweth it out. “Still waters are deep.” Like such deep waters (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.4">Pro 18:4</reference>) is that which a man hath secretly (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.15">Isa 29:15</reference>) planned in his heart. He keeps it secret, conceals it carefully, craftily misleads those who seek to draw it out; but the man of תּבוּנה, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, one who possesses the right criteria for distinguishing between good and bad, true and false, and at the same time has the capacity to look through men and things, draws out (the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. well, ἀνέλξει) the secret עצה, for he penetrates to the bottom of the deep water. Such an one does not deceive himself with men, he knows how to estimate their conduct according to its last underlying motive and aim; and if the purpose is one that is pernicious to him, he meets it in the process of realization. What is here said is applicable not only to the subtle statesman and the general, but also the pragmatical historian and the expositor, as, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, of a poem such as the book of Job, the idea of which lies like a pearl at the bottom of deep water.
entries.890ec3fe1fe54089ec1c223c33084f54b774613f: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.6">Pro 20:6</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.6">6</reference> Almost every one meeteth a man who is gracious to him;    But a man who standeth the test, who findeth such a one? <div eID="gen11402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11403" type="x-p"/> As ציר אמונים, <reference osisRef="Prov.13.17">Pro 13:17</reference>, signifies a messenger in whom there is confidence, and עד אמונים, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.5">Pro 14:5</reference>, a witness who is altogether truthful, so אישׁ אמוּנים is a man who remains true to himself, and maintains fidelity toward others. Such an one it is not easy to find; but patrons who make promises and awaken expectations, finally to leave in the lurch him who depends on them - of such there are many. This contrast would proceed from 6a also, if we took קרא in the sense of to call, to call or cry out with ostentation: <hi type="italic">multi homines sunt quorum suam quisque humanitatem proclamat</hi> (Schelling, Fleischer, Ewald, Zöckler, and also, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Meîri). But אישׁ חסדּו is certainly to be interpreted after <reference osisRef="Prov.11.17">Pro 11:17</reference>, Isa 57:1. Recognising this, Hitzig translates: many a man one names his dear friend; but in point of style this would be as unsuitable as possible. Must יקרא then mean <hi type="italic">vocat</hi>? A more appropriate parallel word to מצא is קרא = קרה, according to which, with Oetinger, Heidenheim, Euchel, and Löwenstein, we explain: the greater part of men meet one who shows himself to them (to this or that man) as אישׁ חסד, a man well-affectioned and benevolent; but it is rare to find one who in his affection and its fruits proves himself to be true, and actually performs that which was hoped for from him. Luther translates, with the Syr. and Targ. after Jerome: <hi type="italic">Viel Menschen werden From gerhümbt</hi> [many men are reputed pious]; but if יקרא were equivalent to יקּרא, then אישׁ חסד ought to have been used instead of אישׁ חסדו. The lxx read רב אדם יקר אישׁ חסד, man is something great, and a compassionate man is something precious; but it costs trouble to find out a true man. The fundamental thought remains almost the same in all these interpretations and readings: love is plentiful; fidelity, rare; therefore חסד, of the right kind, after the image of God, is joined to אמת.
entries.faf59c7e8185fda1db91ed2a663645108a62deb3: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.7">Pro 20:7</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.7">7</reference> He who in his innocence walketh as one upright,    Blessed are his children after him! <div eID="gen11403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11404" type="x-p"/> We may not take the first line as a separate clause with צדּיק, as subject (Van Dyk, Elster) or predicate (Targ.); for, thus rendered, it does not appropriately fall in as parallel to the second line, because containing nothing of promise, and the second line would then strike in at least not so unconnectedly (cf. on the contrary, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.9">Pro 10:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.14.25">Pro 14:25</reference>). We have before us a substantival clause, of which the first line is the complex subject. But Jerome, the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., and Luther erroneously: the just man walking in his innocence; this placing first of the adj. is in opposition to the Hebr. syntax. We must, if the whole is to be interpreted as nom., regard צדיק as permutative: one walking in his innocence, a righteous one. But, without doubt, tsedek is the accus. of the manner; in the manner of one righteous, or in apposition: as one righteous; cf. <reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job 31:26</reference> with Mic 2:7. Thus Hitzig rightly also refers to these two passages, and Ewald also refers to <reference osisRef="Prov.22.11">Pro 22:11</reference>; Pro 24:15. To walk in his innocence as a righteous man, is equivalent to always to do that which is right, without laying claim to any distinction or making any boast on that account; for thereby one only follows the impulse and the direction of his heart, which shows itself and can show itself not otherwise than in unreserved devotion to God and to that which is good. The children after him are not the children after his death (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.67">Gen 24:67</reference>); but, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.4.40">Deu 4:40</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Job.21.21">Job 21:21</reference>, those who follow his example, and thus those who come after him; for already in the lifetime of such an one, the benediction begins to have its fulfilment in his children.
entries.1d363d00d9b40cd1f4d266a225f67a3b04fec930: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.8">Pro 20:8</reference> <div eID="gen11404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11405" type="x-p"/> The following group begins with a royal proverb, which expresses what a king does with his eyes. Two proverbs, of the seeing eye and the necessary opening of the eyes, close it. 8 A king sitting on the seat of justice,    Scattereth asunder all evil with his eyes. <div eID="gen11405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11406" type="x-p"/> Excellently the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. ἐπὶ θρόνου δίκης, for כּסּא־דין is the name of the seat of rectitude (the tribunal), as the “throne of grace,” Heb. 4:17, is the name of the capporeth as the seat of mercy; the seat of the judge is merely called כסא; on the other hand, כסא־דין is the contrast of כּסּא הוּות fo, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.20">Psa 94:20</reference> : the seat from which the decision that is in conformity with what is right (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Jer.5.28">Jer 5:28</reference>) goes forth, and where it is sought. As little here as at <reference osisRef="Prov.20.26">Pro 20:26</reference> is there need for a characterizing adj. to melek; but the lxx hits the meaning for it, understands such to דין: ὅταν βασιλεὺς δίκαιος καθίσῃ ἐπὶ θρόνου. By the “eyes” are we then to understand those of the mind: he sifts, <hi type="italic">dignoscit</hi>, with the eyes of the mind all that is evil, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, distinguishes it subjectively from that which is not evil? Thus Hitzig by a comparison of <reference osisRef="Ps.11.4">Psa 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.139.3">Psa 139:3</reference> (where Jerome has <hi type="italic">eventilasti</hi>, the Vulg. <hi type="italic">investigasti</hi>). Scarcely correctly, for it lies nearer to think on the eyes in the king’s head (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.16.15">Pro 16:15</reference>); in that case: to winnow (to sift) means to separate the good and the bad, but first mediately: to exclude the bad; finally, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.26">Pro 20:26</reference> leads to the conclusion that מזרה is to be understood, not of a subjective, but of an actual scattering, or separating, or driving away. Thus the penetrating, fear-inspiring eyes of the king are meant, as Immanuel explains: בראיית עיניו מבריחם מפניו ומפזר אותם בכל פיאה. But in this explanation the personal rendering of כּל־רע is incorrect; for mezareh, meant of the driving asunder of persons, requires as its object a plur. (cf. 26a). Col-ra is understood as neut. like Pro 5:14. Before the look of a king to whom it belongs to execute righteousness and justice (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.5">Isa 16:5</reference>), nothing evil stands; criminal acts and devices seen through, and so also judged by these eyes, are broken up and scattered to all the winds, along with the danger that thereby threatened the community. It is the command: “put away the evil” (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.6">Deu 13:6</reference> [5]), which the king carries into effect by the powerful influence of his look. With col-ra there is connected the thought that in the presence of the heavenly King no one is wholly free from sin.
