entries.8d48e63a16c86d4f89ccb22e3bfb8f5e19309f87: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.9">Pro 20:9</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.9">9</reference> Who can say I have made my heart clean,    I am pure from my sins? <div eID="gen11406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11407" type="x-p"/> It is the same thought that Solomon expresses in his prayer at the consecration of the temple, 1Ki 8:46 : there is no man who sinneth not. To cleanse his heart (as <reference osisRef="Ps.73.13">Psa 73:13</reference>), is equivalent to to empty it, by self-examination and earnest effort after holiness, of all impure motives and inclinations; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding זכה, to be piercing, shining brightly, cloudlessly pure, Fleischer in Levy’s <hi type="italic">Chald. Wörterbuch</hi>, i. 424. The consequence of זכּות is, becoming pure; and the consequence of זכּות לב, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of the purifying of the heart, the being pure from sinful conduct: I have become pure from my sins, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, from such as I might fall into by not resisting temptations; the suffix is not understood as actual, but as potential, like Psa 18:24. No one can boast of this, for man’s knowledge of himself and of his sins remains always limited (Jer 17:9.; <reference osisRef="Ps.19.13">Psa 19:13</reference>); and sin is so deeply rooted in his nature (<reference osisRef="Job.14.4">Job 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.14-Job.15.16">Job 15:14-16</reference>), that the remains of a sinful tendency always still conceal themselves in the folds of his heart, sinful thoughts still cross his soul, sinful inclinations still sometimes by their natural force overcome the moral resistance that opposes them, and stains of all kinds still defile even his best actions.
entries.2cb1ab29dcb2c5d2d65c4f6e0c91bcfee8817045: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.10">Pro 20:10</reference> <div eID="gen11407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11408" type="x-p"/> This proverb passes sentence of condemnation against gross sins in action and life. <div eID="gen11408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11409" type="x-p"/> Diverse stones, diverse measures - <div eID="gen11409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11410" type="x-p"/> An abomination to Jahve are they both. <div eID="gen11410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11411" type="x-p"/> The stones are, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.11.1">Pro 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.11">Pro 16:11</reference>, those used as weights. Stone and stone, ephah and ephah, means that they are of diverse kinds, one large and one small (the lxx, in which the sequence of the proverbs from <reference osisRef="Prov.20.10">Pro 20:10</reference> is different, has μέγα καὶ μικρόν), so that one may be able deceitfully to substitute the one for the other. איפה (from אפה, to bake) may originally have been used to designate such a quantity of meal as supplied a family of moderate wants; it corresponds to the bath (<reference osisRef="Ezek.45.11">Eze 45:11</reference>) as a measure for fluids, and stands here synecdochically instead of all the measures, including, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the cor, of which the ephah was a tenth part, and the seah, which was a third part of it. 10b = <reference osisRef="Prov.17.5">Pro 17:5</reference>, an echo of <reference osisRef="Lev.19.36">Lev 19:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.25.13">Deu 25:13</reference>-16. Just and equal measure is the demand of a holy God; the contrary is to Him an abhorrence.
entries.14a3d419f4e8a91d6e320d75f38d6a90e3045549: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.11">Pro 20:11</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.11">11</reference> Even a child maketh himself known by his conduct,      Whether his dispostion be pure and whether it be right. <div eID="gen11411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11412" type="x-p"/> If מעלל may be here understood after the use of עולל, to play, to pass the time with anything, then גּם neht  refers thereto: even by his play (Ewald). But granting that מעולל [children], synon. with נער, had occasioned the choice of the word מעלל (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Fleischer on <reference osisRef="Isa.3.4">Isa 3:4</reference>), yet this word never means anything else than work, an undertaking of something, and accomplishing it; wherefore Böttcher proposes מעוּליו, for מעלוּל may have meant play, in contradistinction to מעלל ot noitcni. This is possible, but conjectural. Thus gam is not taken along with b'amalalav. That the child also makes himself known by his actions, is an awkward thought; for if in anything else, in these he must show what one has to expect from him. Thus gam is after the syntactical method spoken of at <reference osisRef="Prov.17.26">Pro 17:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.19.2">Pro 19:2</reference>, to be referred to נער (also the child, even the child), although in this order it is referred to the whole clause. The verb נכר is, from its fundamental thought, to perceive, observe from an ἐναντιόσημον: to know, and to know as strange, to disown (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Isa.3.9">Isa 3:9</reference>); the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. elsewhere signifies, like (Arab.) tankkar, to make oneself unknowable, but here to make oneself knowable; Symmachus, ἐπιγνωρισθήσεται, <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. γνωσθήσεται. Or does the proverb mean: even the child dissembles in his actions (Oetinger)? Certainly not, for that would be a statement which, thus generally made, is not justified by experience. We must then interpret 11b as a direct question, though it has the form of an indirect one: he gives himself to be known, viz., whether his disposition be pure and right. That one may recognise his actions in the conduct of any one, is a platitude; also that one may recognise his conduct in these, is not much better. פּעל is therefore referred by Hitzig to God as the Creator, and he interprets it in the sense of the Arab. khulk, being created = <hi type="italic">natura</hi>. We also in this way explain יצרנוּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.14">Psa 103:14</reference>, as referable to God the יצר; and that <hi type="italic">poal</hi> occurs, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.31">Isa 1:31</reference>, not merely in the sense of action, but also in that of performance or structure, is favourable to this interpretation. But one would think that <hi type="italic">poal</hi>, if thus used in the sense of the nature of man, would have more frequently occurred. It everywhere else means action or work. And thus it is perhaps also here used to denote action, but regarded as habitual conduct, and according to the root-meaning, moral disposition. The N.T. word ἕργον approaches this idea in such passages as Gal 6:4. It is less probable that 11b is understood with reference to the future (Luther and others); for in that case one does not see why the poet did not make use of the more intelligible phrase אם זך וישׁר יהיה פעלו. It is like our (Germ.) proverb: <hi type="italic">Was ein Haken werden will krümmt sick bald</hi> what means to become a hook bends itself early; or: <hi type="italic">Was ein Dörnchen werden will spitzt sich bei Zeiten</hi><note placement="foot">A similar comparison from <hi type="italic">Bereschith Rabba</hi>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Duke’s <hi type="italic">Rabbin. Blumenlese</hi>, p. 126.</note> [what means to become a thorn sharpens itself early], and to the Aram. בוצין בוצין מקטפיה ידיע = that which will become a gourd shows itself in the bud, <hi type="italic">Berachoth</hi> 48a.
entries.52a532dbbccc6a4fc40866e1989ddaae3b74f412: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.12">Pro 20:12</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.12">12</reference> The hearing ear and the seeing eye -      Jahve hath created them both. <div eID="gen11412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11413" type="x-p"/> Löwenstein, like the lxx: the ear hears and the eye sees - it is enough to refer to the contrary to <reference osisRef="Prov.20.10">Pro 20:10</reference> and Pro 17:15. In itself the proverb affirms a fact, and that is its <hi type="italic">sensus simplex</hi>; but besides, this fact may be seen from many points of view, and it has many consequences, none of which is to be rejected as contrary to the meaning: (1.) It lies nearest to draw the conclusion, <hi type="italic">viâ eminentiae</hi>, which is drawn in Psa 94:9. God is thus the All-hearing and the All-seeing, from which, on the one side, the consolation arises that everything that is seen stands under His protection and government, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.3">Pro 15:3</reference>; and on the other side, the warning, <hi type="italic">Aboth</hi> ii. 1: “Know what is above thee; a Seeing eye and a Hearing ear, and all thy conduct is marked in His book.” (2.) With this also is connected the sense arising out of the combination in <reference osisRef="Ps.40.7">Psa 40:7</reference> : man ought then to use the ear and the eye in conformity with the design which they are intended to subserve, according to the purpose of the Creator (Hitzig compares <reference osisRef="Prov.16.4">Pro 16:4</reference>); it is not first applicable to man with reference to the natural, but to the moral life: he shall not make himself deaf and blind to that which it is his duty to hear and to see; but he ought also not to hear and to see with pleasure that from which he should turn away (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.15">Isa 33:15</reference>) - in all his hearing and seeing he is responsible to the Creator of the ear and the eye. (3.) One may thus interpret “hearing” and “seeing” as commendable properties, as Fleischer suggests from comparison of <reference osisRef="Prov.16.11">Pro 16:11</reference> : an ear that truly hears (the word of God and the lessons of Wisdom) and an eye that truly sees (the works of God) are a gift of the Creator, and are (Arab.) lillhi, are to be held as high and precious. Thus the proverb, like a polished gem, may be turned now in one direction and now in another; it is to be regarded as a many-sided fact.
entries.ea28ac7cd8b318eb563406522bb889dec1265aaf: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.13">Pro 20:13</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.13">13</reference> Love not sleep, lest thou become poor;      Open thine eyes, and have enough to eat. <div eID="gen11413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11414" type="x-p"/> What is comprehended in the first line here is presented in detail in <reference osisRef="Prov.6.9">Pro 6:9</reference>-11. The <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. of רוּשׁ, to become poor (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.10.4">Pro 10:4</reference>), is formed metaplastically from ירשׁ, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.21">Pro 23:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.9">Pro 30:9</reference>, as at <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.7">1Sa 2:7</reference>; Hitzig compares (Arab.) ryth, which, however, means to loiter or delay, not to come back or down. The R. רש signifies either to be slack without support (cf. דּל), or to desire (cf. אבון, Arab. fkyr, properly <hi type="italic">hiscens</hi>, R. פק, as in פקח, to open widely, which here follows). Regarding the second imper. 13b, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.3.4">Pro 3:4</reference> : it has the force of a consequence, <hi type="italic">Las deine augen wacker sein, So wirstu brots gnug haben</hi> (Luth.) [Let thine eyes be open, so shalt thou have bread enough]. With these two proverbs of the eyes, the group beginning with <reference osisRef="Prov.20.8">Pro 20:8</reference> rounds itself off.
entries.1747741270c538bab273384647d76248fa10ca8e: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.14">Pro 20:14</reference> <div eID="gen11414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11415" type="x-p"/> The following group has its natural limit at the new point of departure at <reference osisRef="Prov.20.20">Pro 20:20</reference>, and is internally connected in a diversity of ways. 14 “Bad, bad!” saith the buyer;      And going his way, he boasteth then. <div eID="gen11415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11416" type="x-p"/> Luther otherwise: “Bad, bad!” saith one if he hath it; <div eID="gen11416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11417" type="x-p"/> But when it is gone, then he boasteth of it. <div eID="gen11417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11418" type="x-p"/> This rendering has many supporters. Geier cites the words of the Latin poet: <div eID="gen11418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11419" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Omne bonum praesens minus est, sperata videntur Magna</hi>.” <div eID="gen11419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11420" type="x-p"/> Schultens quotes the proverbs τὸ παρὸν βαρύ and <hi type="italic">Praesentia laudato</hi>, for with Luther he refers ואזל לו to the present possession (אזל, as <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.7">1Sa 9:7</reference> = (Arab.) zâl, to cease, to be lost), and translates: <hi type="italic">at dilapsum sibi, tum demum pro splendido celebrat</hi>. But by this the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. does not receive its full meaning; and to extract from הקּונה the idea to which ואזל לו refers, if not unnecessary, is certainly worthless. Hakkoneh may also certainly mean the possessor, but the possessor by acquisition (lxx and the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. ὁ κτώμενος); for the most part it signifies the possessor by purchase, the buyer (Jerome, <hi type="italic">emptor</hi>), as correlate of מכר, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.2">Isa 24:2</reference>; Eze 4:12. It is customary for the buyer to undervalue that which he seeks to purchase, so as to obtain it as cheaply as possible; afterwards he boasts that he has bought that which is good, and yet so cheap. That is an every-day experience; but the proverb indirectly warns against conventional lying, and shows that one should not be startled and deceived thereby. The subject to ואזל לו is thus the buyer; אזל with לו denotes, more definitely even than הלך לו, going from thence, s'en aller. Syntactically, the punctuation ואזל לו [and he takes himself off] (<hi type="italic">perf. hypoth</hi>., Ewald, 357a) would have been near (Jerome: <hi type="italic">et cum recesserit</hi>); but yet it is not necessary, with Hitzig, thus to correct it. The poet means to say: making himself off, he then boasts. We cannot in German place the “<hi type="italic">alsdann</hi>” [then] as the אז here, and as also, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, at <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.12">1Sa 20:12</reference>; but Theodotion, in good Greek: καὶ πορευθεὶς τότε καυχήσεται. We may write ואזל לו with <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> on the antepenult, on which the accent is thrown back, cf. חונן, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.17">Pro 19:17</reference>, but not לּו; for the rule for <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> does not here, with the retrogression of the tone, come into application, as, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, in אוכל לּחמי, Psa 41:10. Singularly the Syr. and Targ. do not read רע רע, but רע לרע, and couple <reference osisRef="Prov.20.15">Pro 20:15</reference> with 14. In the lxx, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.14-Prov.20.19">Pro 20:14-19</reference> are wanting.
entries.dec9bd683717113948bdd3a0be7007a864253b40: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.15">Pro 20:15</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.15">15</reference> There is indeed gold, and many pearls;      But a precious treasure are lips full of knowledge. <div eID="gen11420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11421" type="x-p"/> In order to find a connection between this proverb and that which precedes, we need only be reminded of the parable of the merchantman who sought goodly pearls, Mat 13:45. The proverb rises to a climax: there is gold, and there are pearls in abundance, the one of which has always a higher value than the other; but intelligent lips are above all such jewels - they are a precious treasure, which gold and all pearls cannot equal. In a similar manner the N.T. places the one pearl above the many goodly pearls. So might דעת (chokma) be called the pearl above all pearls (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.15">Pro 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.8.11">Pro 8:11</reference>); but the lips as the organ of knowledge are fittingly compared with a precious vessel, a vessel of more precious substance than gold and pearls are.
entries.2ff829fe2de70a1213af38a6eeb4ed2262525871: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.16">Pro 20:16</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.16">16</reference> Take from him the garment, for he hath become surety for another;      And for strangers take him as a pledge. <div eID="gen11421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11422" type="x-p"/> The same proverb <reference osisRef="Prov.27.13">Pro 27:13</reference>, where קח, with the usual aphaeresis, here interchanges with it the fuller form לקח, which is also found at Eze 37:16. To this imperative חבלהוּ is parallel: take him as a pledge (Theodotion, Jerome, the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. and Luther); it is not a substantive: his pledge (Targ.), which would require the word חבלתו (חבלו); nor is it to be read with the Syr. חבלהוּ, one pledges him; but it is imperative, not however of the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, which would be חבלהוּ, and would mean “destroy him;” but, as Aben Ezra rightly, the imperative of <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> of חבל, to take as a pledge, <reference osisRef="Exod.22.25">Exo 22:25</reference>, for חבלהוּ without any example indeed except חננני, <reference osisRef="Ps.9.14">Psa 9:14</reference>; cf. Psa 80:16. The first line is clear: take his garment, for he has become good for another (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.11.15">Pro 11:15</reference>), who has left him in the lurch, so that he must now become wise by experience. The second line also is intelligible if we read, according to the Chethı̂b, נכרים (Jerome, the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>.), not נכריּם, as Schultens incorrectly points it, and if we interpret this plur. like בנים, <reference osisRef="Gen.21.7">Gen 21:7</reference>, with Hitzig following Luther, as plur. of the category: take him as a pledge, hold fast by his person, so as not to suffer injury from strange people for whom he has become surety. But the Kerı̂ requires נכריּה (according to which Theodotion and the Syr., and, more distinctly still than these, the Targ. translates), and thus, indeed, it stands written, <reference osisRef="Prov.27.13">Pro 27:13</reference>, without the Kerı̂, thus Bathra 173b reads and writes also here. Either נכריּה is a strange woman, a prostitute, a <hi type="italic">maitresse</hi> for whom the unwise has made himself surety, or it is neut. for <hi type="italic">aliena res</hi> (lxx <reference osisRef="Prov.27.13">Pro 27:13</reference>, τὰ ἀλλότρια), a matter not properly belonging to this unwise person. We regard נכרים in this passage as original. בעד coincides with <reference osisRef="Prov.6.26">Pro 6:26</reference> : it does not mean ἀντὶ, but ὑπέρ; “for strange people” is here equivalent to for the sake of, on account of strange people” is here equivalent to for the sake of, on account of strange people (χάριν τῶν ἀλλοτρίων, as the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. translates it).
entries.07ea0b1f9f68716202701fe2deae41e2985a4a71: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.17">Pro 20:17</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.17">17</reference> Sweet to a man is the bread of deceit;      Yet at last his mouth is full of gravel. “Bread of deceit” is not deceit itself, as that after which the desire of a man goes forth, and that for which he has a relish (thus, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Immanuel and Hitzig); but that which is not gained by labour, and is not merited. Possession (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.4.17">Pro 4:17</reference>) or enjoyment (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.17">Pro 9:17</reference>) obtained by deceit is thus called, as לחם כּזבים, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.3">Pro 23:3</reference>, denotes bread; but for him who has a relish for it, it is connected with deceit. Such bread of lies is sweet to a man, because it has come to him without effort, but in the end not only will he have nothing to eat, but his tongue, teeth, and mouth will be injured by small stones; <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, in the end he will have nothing, and there will remain to him only evil (Fleischer). Or: it changes itself (<reference osisRef="Job.20.14">Job 20:14</reference>) at last into gravel, of which his mouth is filled full, as we might say, “it lies at last in his stomach like lead.” חצץ is the Arab. ḥaṭny, gravel (Hitzig, <hi type="italic">grien</hi> = <hi type="italic">gries</hi>, coarse sand, grit), R. חץ, <hi type="italic">scindere</hi>. Similarly in Arab. ḥajar, a stone, is used as the image of disappointed expectations, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the adulterer finds a stone, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, experiences disappointment.
entries.7eb94540ea5a7e196ba6cf37b2f5461e4fbef380: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.18">Pro 20:18</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.18">18</reference> Plans are established by counsel,      And with prudent government make war. <div eID="gen11422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11423" type="x-p"/> From the conception of a thought, practically influencing the formation of our own life and the life of the community, to its accomplishment there is always a long way which does not lead to the end unless one goes forward with counsel and strength combined, and considers all means and eventualities. The <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. of כּוּן means, in a passive sense: to be accomplished or realized (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.2">Psa 141:2</reference>). The clause 18a is true for times of war as well as for times of peace; war is disastrous, unless it is directed with strategic skill (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding תּחבּות, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.5">Pro 1:5</reference>). Grotius compares the proverb, Γνῶμαι πλέον δρατοῦσιν ἢ σθένος χειρῶν. In <reference osisRef="Prov.24.6">Pro 24:6</reference>, the necessity of counsel is also referred to the case of war. Ewald would read [the infin.] עשׂה, or עשׂה: with management it is that one carries on war. But why? Because to him the challenge to carry on war appears to be contrary to the spirit of proverbial poetry. But the author of the proverb does certainly mean: if thou hast to carry on war, carry it on with the skill of a general; and the imper. is protected by <reference osisRef="Prov.24.6">Pro 24:6</reference> against that infin., which is, besides, stylistically incongruous.
entries.3476d739c39453a4a697d5309d60cd2de93b3fe1: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.19">Pro 20:19</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.19">19</reference> He that goeth out gossiping revealeth a secret;      And the babbler have nothing to do. <div eID="gen11423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11424" type="x-p"/> Luther otherwise (like Hitzig) - <div eID="gen11424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11425" type="x-p"/> Be not complicated with him who revealeth a secret, <div eID="gen11425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11426" type="x-p"/> And with the slanderer, and with the false (better: loquacious) mouth, so that ל and the warning apply to the threefold description, a rendering which Kimchi also, and Immanuel, and others at least suggest. But in connection with <reference osisRef="Prov.11.13">Pro 11:13</reference>, the first line has the force of a <hi type="italic">judicium</hi>, which includes the warning to entrust nothing to a babbler which ought to be kept silent. Write גּולה סּוד, as found in Codd. and old Edd., with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> on the penultima, on which the tone is thrown back, and <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> to ס, after the rule of the דחיק (Gesen. §20, 2a), altogether like קונה לב, Pro 15:32. 19b the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. translates after the first meaning of the word by Kimchi, τῷ ἀπαταιῶνι τοῖς χείλεσι, to him who slanders and befools, for it thus improves Theodotion’s τῷ ἀπατῶντι τὰ χείλη αὐτοῦ. But פּתה means, <reference osisRef="Job.5.2">Job 5:2</reference> - cf. Hos 7:11 - not him who befools another, but him who is befooled, is slandered, by another (Aben Ezra: שׁיפתוהו אחרים), with which שׂפתיו here does not agree. But now he who is easily befooled is called פּתה, as being open to influence (susceptible), <hi type="italic">patens</hi>; and if this particip. is used, as here, transitively, and, on account of the object שׂפתיו standing near cannot possibly be equivalent to מפתּה, the usage of the language also just noticed is against it, then it means <hi type="italic">patefaciens</hi> or <hi type="italic">dilatans</hi> (cf. הפתּה, <reference osisRef="Gen.9.27">Gen 9:27</reference>, Targ. אפתּי = הרחיב), and places itself as synon. to פשׂק, <reference osisRef="Prov.13.3">Pro 13:3</reference>; thus one is called who does not close his mouth, who cannot hold his mouth, who always idly babbles, and is therefore, because he can keep nothing to himself, a dangerous companion. The Complut. rightly translates: μετὰ πλατύνοντος τὰ ἑαυτοῦ μὴ μίχθητι χείλη.
entries.19fe195f02524e7e84c896eed32a50965242defa: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.20">Pro 20:20</reference> <div eID="gen11426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11427" type="x-p"/> The following group begins, for once more the aim of this older Book of Proverbs becomes prominent, with an inculcation of the fourth<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, The <hi type="italic">fifth</hi> according to the arrangement of the Westminster Confession.</note> commandment. 20 He that curseth his father and his mother,      His light is extinguished in midnight darkness. <div eID="gen11427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11428" type="x-p"/> The divine law, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.17">Exo 21:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.20.9">Lev 20:9</reference>, condemns such an one to death. But the proverb does not mean this sentence against the criminal, which may only seldom be carried into execution, but the fearful end which, because of the righteousness of God ruling in history, terminates the life of such an unnatural son (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.17">Pro 30:17</reference>). Of the godless, it has already been said that their light is extinguished, <reference osisRef="Prov.13.9">Pro 13:9</reference>, there is suddenly an end to all that brightened, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, made happy and embellished their life; but he who acts wickedly (קלּל, R. קל, <hi type="italic">levem esse</hi>, synon. הקלה, <reference osisRef="Deut.27.16">Deu 27:16</reference>), even to the cursing of his father and mother, will see himself surrounded by midnight darkness (Symmachus, σκοτομήνῃ, moonless night), not: he will see himself in the greatest need, forsaken by divine protection (Fleischer), for Jansen rightly: <hi type="italic">Lux et lucerna in scripturis et vitae claritatem et posteritatem et prosperitatem significat</hi>. The apple of the eye, אישׁון, of darkness (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.7.9">Pro 7:9</reference>), is that which forms the centre of centralization of darkness. The Syr. renders it correctly by bobtho, pupil of the eye, but the Targ. retains the אשׁוּן of the Kerı̂, and renders it in Aram. by אתוּן, which Rashi regards as an infin., Parchon as a particip. after the form ערוּך; but it may be also an infin. substantive after the form עזוּז, and is certainly nothing else than the abbreviated and vocally obscured אישׁון. For the Talm. אשׁן, to be hard, furnishes no suitable idea; and the same holds true of אשׁוּני, times, <reference osisRef="Lev.15.25">Lev 15:25</reference> of the Jerusalem Targ.; while the same abbreviation and the same passing over of <hi type="italic">o</hi> into <hi type="italic">u</hi> represents this as the inflected אישׁון (= עת). There is also no evidence for a verb אשׁן, to be black, dark; the author of Aruch interprets אשׁונא, <hi type="italic">Bereschith Rabba</hi>, c. 33, with reference to the passage before us, of a dark bathing apartment, but only tentatively, and אישׁון is there quoted as the Targ. of צל, <reference osisRef="Gen.19.8">Gen 19:8</reference>, which the text lying before us does not ratify. Ishon means the little man (in the eye), and neither the blackness (Buxtorf and others) nor the point of strength, the central point (Levy) of the eye.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Fleischer in Levy’s <hi type="italic">Chald. Wörterbuch</hi>, i. 419.</note>
entries.3c714a37447148ddc2fe31a85edca245d6c06866: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.21">Pro 20:21</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.21">21</reference> An inheritance which in the beginning is obtained in haste,      Its end will not be blessed. <div eID="gen11428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11429" type="x-p"/> The partic. מבחל may, after Zec 11:8, cf. Syr. bhlaa', <hi type="italic">nauseans</hi>, mean “detested,” but that affords here no sense; rather it might be interpreted after the Arab. bajila, to be avaricious, “gotten by avarice, niggardliness,” with which, however, neither נחלה, inheritance, nor, since avarice is a chronic disease, בּראשׁונה agrees. On the contrary, the Kerı̂ מבהלת [hastened] perfectly agrees, both linguistically (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.28.22">Pro 28:22</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.13.11">Pro 13:11</reference>) and actually; for, as Hitzig remarks, the words following <reference osisRef="Prov.20.20">Pro 20:20</reference> fully harmonize with the idea of an inheritance, into the possession of which one is put before it is rightly due to him; for a son such as that, the parents may live too long, and so he violently deprives them of the possession (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.19.26">Pro 19:26</reference>); but on such a possession there rests no blessing. Since the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> may mean to hasten, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.9">Est 2:9</reference>, so מבהל may mean hastened = speedy, <reference osisRef="Esth.8.14">Est 8:14</reference>, as well as made in haste. All the old interpreters adopt the Kerı̂; the Aram. render it well by מסרהבא, from מסרהב, overturned; and Luther, like Jerome, <hi type="italic">haereditas ad quam festinatur</hi>.
entries.949f969de2bb6859d5df260a32105359b5350ab4: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.22">Pro 20:22</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.22">22</reference> Say not: I will avenge the evil;      Hope in Jahve, so will He help thee. <div eID="gen11429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11430" type="x-p"/> Men ought always to act toward their neighbours according to the law of love, and not according to the <hi type="italic">jus talionis</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.29">Pro 24:29</reference>; they ought not only, by requiting good with evil (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.13">Pro 16:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.7.5">Psa 7:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.12">Psa 35:12</reference>), not to transgress this law of requital, but they ought to surpass it, by also recompensing not evil with evil (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding שׁלּם, and synon. to <reference osisRef="Prov.17.13">Pro 17:13</reference>); and that is what the proverb means, for 22b supposes injustice suffered, which might stir up a spirit of revenge. It does not, however, say that men ought to commit the taking of vengeance to God; but, in the sense of <reference osisRef="Rom.12.17-Rom.12.19">Rom 12:17-19</reference>; 1Pe 3:9, that, renouncing all dependence on self, they ought to commit their deliverance out of the distress into which they have fallen, and their vindication, into the hands of God; for the promise is not that He will avenge them, but that He will help them. The jussive וישׁע (write וישׁע, according to <hi type="italic">Metheg-setzung</hi>, §42, with <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> as העמדה, with the ע to secure distinct utterance to the final guttural) states as a consequence, like, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, 2Ki 5:10, what will then happen (Jerome, Luther, Hitzig) if one lets God rule (Gesen. §128, 2c); equally possible, syntactically, is the rendering: that He may help thee (lxx, Ewald); but, regarded as a promise, the words are more in accordance with the spirit of the proverb, and they round it off more expressively.
entries.22b30ff1df62bfd8783d1090d812651b70acad0c: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.23">Pro 20:23</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.23">23</reference> An abomination to Jahve are two kinds of weights;      And deceitful balances are not good. <div eID="gen11430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11431" type="x-p"/> A variant to <reference osisRef="Prov.20.10">Pro 20:10</reference>, Pro 11:1. The pred. לא־טוב (<reference osisRef="Prov.17.26">Pro 17:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.18.5">Pro 18:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.19.3">Pro 19:3</reference>) is conceived of as neut.; they are not good, much rather bad and pernicious, for the deceiver succeeds only in appearance; in reality he fails.
entries.1a90bad5876809c558c178449b1a1711e5466abf: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.24">Pro 20:24</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.24">24</reference> The steps of a man depend on Jahve;      And a man - how can he understand his way? <div eID="gen11431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11432" type="x-p"/> Line first is from <reference osisRef="Ps.37.23">Psa 37:23</reference>, but there, where the clause has the verbal predicate כּוננוּ, the meaning is that it is the gracious assistance of God, by virtue of which a man takes certain steps with his feet, while here we have before us a variation of the proverb “<hi type="italic">der Mensch denkt, Gott lenkt</hi>” = man proposes, God disposes, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.9">Pro 16:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.23">Jer 10:23</reference>; for מן, as at <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.37">2Sa 3:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.23">Psa 118:23</reference>, denotes God in general as conditioning, as the ultimate cause. Man is indeed free to turn himself hither or thither, to decide on this course of conduct or on that, and is therefore responsible for it; but the relations co-operating in all his steps as the possible and defining conditions are God’s contrivance and guidance, and the consequences which are connected with his steps and flow therefrom, lie beyond the power of man - every one of his steps is a link of a chain, neither the beginning nor the end of which he can see; while, on the other hand, God’s knowledge comprehends the beginning, middle, and end, and the wisdom of God ruling in the sphere of history, makes all human activity, the free action of man, subservient to his world-plan. The question, which has a negative answer, is applicable to man: what, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, how shall he understand his way? מה is like, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Exod.10.26">Exo 10:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.2">Job 9:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.28">Job 19:28</reference>, accus., and fluctuates between the functions of a governed accusative: What does he understand... (<reference osisRef="Job.11.8">Job 11:8</reference>) and an adv.: how, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, how so little, how even not, for it is the מה of the negative question which has become in (Arab.) mâ a word of negation. The way of a man is his life's-course. This he understands in the present life only relatively, the true unravelling of it remains for the future.
entries.be58c4312f5be7dc52dc3f01b4a75f7b401e131e: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.25">Pro 20:25</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.25">25</reference> It is a snare to a man to cry out hastily “holy;”      And first after vows to investigate. <div eID="gen11432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11433" type="x-p"/> Two other interpretations of the first line have been proposed. The snare of a man devours, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, destroys the holy; but then מוקשׁ אדם must be an expression of an action, instead of an expression of an endurance, which is impossible. The same is true against the explanation: the snare of a man devours, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, consumes, eats up the holy, which as such is withdrawn from common use. Jerome with his <hi type="italic">devotare sanctos</hi>, and Luther with his <hi type="italic">das Heilige lestern</hi> [to calumniate the holy], give to לוּע = בּלע a meaning which loses itself in the arbitrary. Accordingly, nothing is to be done with the meaning καταπίεται (Aquila, the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>.). But ילע will be the abbreviated fut. of לוּע (from ילוּע), or לעע (ילע), <reference osisRef="Job.6.3">Job 6:3</reference> = (Arab.) laghâ <hi type="italic">temere loqui</hi> (<hi type="italic">proloqui</hi>); and קדשׁ (after Hitzig: consecration, which is contrary to usage) is like κορβᾶν, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.11">Mar 7:11</reference>, the exclamation to which one suddenly gives utterance, thereby meaning that this or that among his possessions henceforth no longer belongs to him, but is consecrated to God, and thus ought to be delivered up to the temple. Such a sudden vow and halting deference to the oath that has been uttered is a snare to a man, for he comes to know that he has injured himself by the alienation of his property, which he has vowed beyond that which was due from him, or that the fulfilling of his vow is connected with difficulties, and perhaps also to others, with regard to whom its disposal was not permitted to him, is of evil consequences, or it may be he is overcome by repentance and is constrained to break his oath. The lxx hits the true meaning of the proverb with rare success: Παγὶς ἀνδρὶ ταχύ τι τῶν ἰδίων ἁγιάσαι, μετὰ δὲ τὸ εὔξασθαι μετανοεῖν γίνεται. נדרים is plur. of the category (cf. 16b Chethı̂b), and בקּר, as 2Ki 16:15, Arab. baḳr, <hi type="italic">examinare, inquirere</hi>, means to subject to investigation, viz., whether he ought to observe, and might observe, a vow such as this, or whether he might not and ought not rather to renounce it (Fleischer). Viewed syntactically, 25a is so difficult, that Bertheau, with Hitzig, punctuates ילע; but this substantive must be formed from a verb ילע (cf. <reference osisRef="Hab.3.13">Hab 3:13</reference>), and this would mean, after (Arab.) wala', “to long eagerly for,” which is not suitable here. The punctuation shows ילע as the 3rd fut. What interpreters here say of the doubled accent of the word arises from ignorance: the correct punctuation is ילע, with <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> to ע, to give the final guttural more force in utterance. The poet appears to place in the foreground: “a snare for a man,” as a <hi type="italic">rubrum</hi>; and then continuing the description, he cries out suddenly “holy!” and after the vow, he proceeds to deliberate upon it. Fleischer rightly: <hi type="italic">post vota inquisiturus est</hi> (<hi type="italic">in ea</hi>) = יהיה לבקּר; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Hab.1.17">Hab 1:17</reference>, which passage Hitzig also compares as syntactically very closely related.
entries.e9e48edcd3f6445892019aa4d2730d1432555735: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.26">Pro 20:26</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.26">26</reference> A wise king winnoweth the godless,      And bringeth over them the wheel. <div eID="gen11433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11434" type="x-p"/> A variant to <reference osisRef="Prov.20.8">Pro 20:8</reference>, but here with the following out of the figure of the winnowing. For אופן with מזרה is, without doubt, the wheel of the threshing-cart, עגלה, Isa 28:27.; and thus with מזרה, the winnowing fork, מזרה is to be thought of; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., a description of them along with that of the winnowing shovel, רחת, in Wetzstein’s <hi type="italic">Excursus</hi> to Isa., p. 707ff. We are not to think of the punishment of the wheel, which occurs only as a terrible custom of war (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Amos.1.3">Amo 1:3</reference>). It is only meant that a wise king, by sharp and vigorous procedure, separates the godless, and immediately visits them with merited punishment, as he who works with the winnowing shovel gives the chaff to the wind. Most ancient interpreters think on אופן (from אפן, <hi type="italic">vertere</hi>) in its metaphorical meaning: τρόπος (thus also Löwenstein, he deals with them according to merit), or the wheel of fortune, with reference to the constellations; thus, misfortune (Immanuel, Meîri). Arama, Oetinger, and others are, however, on the right track.
entries.fcfbebf3b86aaf36745f5a01cd76e718a10370c4: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.27">Pro 20:27</reference> <div eID="gen11434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11435" type="x-p"/> With a proverb of a light that was extinguished, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.20">Pro 20:20</reference> began the group; the proverb of God’s light, which here follows, we take as the beginning of a new group. 27 A candle of Jahve is the soul of man,      Searching through all the chambers of the heart. <div eID="gen11435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11436" type="x-p"/> If the O.T. language has a separate word to denote the self-conscious personal human spirit in contradistinction to the spirit of a beast, this word, according to the usage of the language, as Reuchlin, in an appendix to Aben Ezra, remarks, is נשׁמה; it is so called as the principle of life breathed immediately by God into the body (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Gen 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.7.22">Gen 7:22</reference>). Indeed, that which is here said of the human spirit would not be said of the spirit of a beast: it is “the mystery of self-consciousness which is here figuratively represented” (Elster). The proverb intentionally does not use the word נפשׁ, for this is not the power of self-consciousness in man, but the medium of bodily life; it is related secondarily to nshmh (רוח), while נשׁמת חיים (רוח) is used, נפשׁ חיים is an expression unheard of. Hitzig is in error when he understands by נשׁמה here the soul in contradistinction to the spirit, and in support of this appeals to an expression in the <hi type="italic">Cosmography</hi> of <hi type="italic">Kazwîni</hi>: “the soul (Arab. âl-nefs) is like the lamp which moves about in the chambers of the house;” here also en-nefs is the self-conscious spirit, for the Arab. and post-bibl. Heb. terminology influenced by philosophy reverses the biblical usage, and calls the rational soul נפשׁ, and, on the contrary, the animal soul נשׁמה, רוח (<hi type="italic">Psychologie</hi>, p. 154). חפשׂ is the particip. of חפּשׂ, Zep 1:12, without distinguishing the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> and <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>. Regarding חדרי־בטן, lxx ταμιεῖα κοιλίας, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.18.8">Pro 18:8</reference> : בּטן denotes the inner part of the body (R. בט, to be deepened), and generally of the personality; cf. Arab. bâtn âlrwh, the interior of the spirit, and <reference osisRef="Prov.22.18">Pro 22:18</reference>, according to which Fleischer explains: “A candle of Jahve, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, a means bestowed on man by God Himself to search out the secrets deeply hid in the spirit of another.” But the candle which God has kindled in man has as the nearest sphere of illumination, which goes forth from it, the condition of the man himself - the spirit comprehends all that belongs to the nature of man in the unity of self-consciousness, but yet more: it makes it the object of reflection; it penetrates, searching it through, and seeks to take it up into its knowledge, and recognises the problem proposed to it, to rule it by its power. The proverb is thus to be ethically understood: the spirit is that which penetrates that which is within, even into its many secret corners and folds, with its self-testing and self-knowing light - it is, after <reference osisRef="Matt.6.22">Mat 6:22</reference>, the inner light, the inner eye. Man becomes known to himself according to his moral as well as his natural condition in the light of the spirit; “for what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him?” says Paul, 1Co 2:11. With reference to this Solomonic proverb, the seven-branched candlestick is an ancient symbol of the soul, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, on the Jewish sepulchral monuments of the Roman <hi type="italic">viâ Portuensis</hi>. Our texts present the phrase נר יהוה; but the Talm. <hi type="italic">Pesachim</hi> 7b, 8a, the <hi type="italic">Pesikta</hi> in part 8, the Midrash <hi type="italic">Othijoth de-Rabbi Akiba</hi>, under the letter נ, Alphasi (יף''ר) in <hi type="italic">Pesachim</hi>, and others, read נר אלהים; and after this phrase the Targum translates, while the Syr. and the other old versions render by the word “Lord” (<hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. ὀντωτής), and thus had יהוה before them.
entries.1404ab5129a3f86f57071257fde701ebb21454ea: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.28">Pro 20:28</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.28">28</reference> Love and truth guard the king;      And he supports his throne by love. <div eID="gen11436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11437" type="x-p"/> We have not in the German [nor in the Eng.] language a couple of words that completely cover חסד ואמת; when they are used of God, we translate them by grace and truth [<hi type="italic">Gnade u. Wahrheit</hi>], <reference osisRef="Ps.40.12">Psa 40:12</reference> (יצּרוּני); when of men, by love and truth [<hi type="italic">Liebe u. Treue</hi>], <reference osisRef="Prov.16.6">Pro 16:6</reference>; and when of the two-sided divine forces, by kindness and truth, Pro 3:3. Love and truth are the two good spirits that guard the king. If it is elsewhere said that the king’s throne is supported “with judgment and with justice,” <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Isa 9:6</reference> [7]; here, on the other side, we see that the exercise of government must have love as its centre; he has not only to act on the line of right, שׁוּרת הדּין; but, as the later proverb says, in such a way, that within this circle his conduct is determined by the central motive of love. In this sense we give the king not only the title of <hi type="italic">Grossmächtigster</hi> [most high and mighty], but also that of “<hi type="italic">Allergnädigster</hi>” most gracious, for the king can and ought to exercise grace before other men; the virtue of condescension establishes his throne more than the might of greatness.
entries.c19e7477d967066569650b5047ffd3833ff7a5c7: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.29">Pro 20:29</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.29">29</reference> The ornament of young men is their strength;      And the honour of the old is grey hairs. <div eID="gen11437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11438" type="x-p"/> Youth has the name בּחוּר (different from בּחוּר, chosen), of the maturity (R. בחר, cogn. בכר, בגר, whence Mishn. בּגרוּת, manhood, in contradistinction to נערוּת) into which he enters from the bloom of boyhood; and the old man is called זקן (Arab. dhikn, as Schultens says, <hi type="italic">a mento pendulo</hi>, from the hanging chin זקן, (Arab.) dhakan, chin, beard on the chin). To stand in the fulness of fresh unwasted strength is to youth, as such, an ornament (תּפארת, cf. פּארוּר, blooming colour of the countenance); on the contrary, to the old man who has spent his strength in the duties of his office, or as it is said at <reference osisRef="Prov.16.31">Pro 16:31</reference>, “in the way of righteousness,” grey hairs (שׂיבה, from שׂב, Arab. shâb, <hi type="italic">canescere</hi>) give an honourable appearance (הדר, from הדר, <hi type="italic">turgidum, amplum esse</hi>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Isa.63.1">Isa 63:1</reference>).
entries.d7bdc4acd4bcb47973975e50667932cbc615e0e4: <reference osisRef="Prov.20.30">Pro 20:30</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.30">30</reference> Cutting wounds cleanse away evil,      And reach the inner parts of the body. <div eID="gen11438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11439" type="x-p"/> The two words for wounds in line first stand in the <hi type="italic">st. constr</hi>.; חבּוּרה (from חבר, to be bound around with stripes, to be striped) is properly the streak, the stripe; but is here heightened by פּצע (from פּצע, to cleave, split, tear open), beyond the idea of the stripe-wound: tearing open the flesh, cuts tearing into the flesh. The pred. is after the Kerı̂ תּמרוּק; but this substantive, found in the Book of Esther, where it signifies the purification of the women for the harem (according to which, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Ahron B. Joseph explains כמו תמרוק לנשׁים שׁהוא יפה להם), is syntactically hard, and scarcely original. For if we explain with Kimchi: wounds of deep incision find their cleansing (cure) by evil, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, by means which bring suffering (according to which, probably the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. μώλωπες τραύματος λάμψουσιν ἐν κακῷ), then תמרוקן, with the pronoun pointing back, one would have expected. But the interpretation of בּרע, of severe means of cure, is constrained; that which lies nearest, however, is to understand רע of evil. But if, with this understanding of the word, we translate: <hi type="italic">Vibices plagarum sunt lustratio quae adhibetur malo</hi> (Fleischer), one does not see why בּרע, and not rather gen. רע, is used. But if we read after the Chethı̂b תּמריק, then all is syntactically correct; for (1.) that the word ימריקוּ, or תּמרקנה, is not used, is in accordance with a well-known rule, Gesen. §146. 3; and (2.) that המריק is connected, not directly with an accus. obj., but with ב, has its analogy in התעה ב, <reference osisRef="Jer.42.2">Jer 42:2</reference>, השׁרישׁ בּ, <reference osisRef="Job.31.12">Job 31:12</reference>, and the like, and besides has its special ground in the metaphorical character of the cleansing. Thus, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, one uses Syr. 't'aa' of external misleading; but with Syr. k of moral misleading (Ewald, §217, 2); and Arab. '  of erecting a building; but with Arab. b of the intellectual erection of a memorial (monument). It is the so-called Bâ̇âlmojâz; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., de Sacy’s <hi type="italic">Chrest Arab</hi>. i. 397. The verb מרק means in Talm. also, “to take away” (a metaph. of <hi type="italic">abstergere</hi>; cf. Arab. marak, to wipe off)<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Dozy’s <hi type="italic">Lettre à M. Fleischer</hi> (1871), p. 198.</note> and that meaning is adopted, <hi type="italic">Schabbath </hi> 33a, for the interpretations of this proverb: stripes and wounds a preparedness for evil carries away, and sorrow in the innermost part of the body, which is explained by דרוקן (a disease appearing in diverse forms; cf. “<hi type="italic">Drachenschuss</hi>,”; as the name of an animal disease); but granting that the biblical מרק may bear this meaning, the ב remains unaccountable; for we say מרק עצמו לעברה, for to prepare oneself for a transgression (sin of excess), and not בעברה. We have thus to abide by the primary meaning, and to compare the proverb, <hi type="italic">Berachoth</hi> 5a: “afflictive providences wash away all the transgressions of a man.” But the proverb before us means, first at least, not the wounds which God inflicts, but those which human educational energy inflicts: deep-cutting wounds, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, stern discipline, leads to the rubbing off of evil, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, rubs it, washes it, cleanses it away. It may now be possible that in 30b the subject idea is permutatively continued: <hi type="italic">et verbera penetralium corporis</hi> (thus the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>.: πληγαὶ τῶν ταμιείων τοῦ γαρστρός), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, <hi type="italic">quorum vis ad intimos corporis et animi recessus penetrat</hi> (Fleischer). But that is encumbered, and חדרי־בטן (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.20.27">Pro 20:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.8">Pro 18:8</reference>), as referring to the depths to which stern corporal discipline penetrates, has not its full force. וּמכּות is either a particip.: and that is touching (<hi type="italic">ferientes</hi>) the inner chambers of the body, or חדרי־בטן is with the ב, or immediately the second object of תמריק to be supplied: and strokes (rub off, cleanse, make pure) the innermost part. Jerome and the Targ. also supply ב, but erroneously, as designating place: <hi type="italic">in secretioribus ventris</hi>, relatively better the lxx and Syr.: εἰς ταμιεῖα κοιλίας. Luther hits the sense at least, for he translates: <div eID="gen11439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11440" type="x-p"/> One must restrain evil with severe punishment, <div eID="gen11440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11441" type="x-p"/> And with hard strokes which one feels.  <chapter eID="Prov.20"/>

                  <ns0:p n="12">12 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 4. 11.                   <ns0:p n="13">13 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 6. 9. & 12. 14. & 19. 15.</ns0:note> Love not sleep <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e</ns0:hi> Immoderate sleep, or sloth or idleness.                   <ns0:p n="14">14 <ns0:hi>It is</ns0:hi> naught <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The commodity is but of little worth.</ns0:note>, it is naught saith the buyer <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">To wit, to the Seller: he discommends it that he may bring down the price of it.</ns0:note>, but when he is gone his way <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">With the commodity purchased.</ns0:note>, then he boasteth <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">That by his wit he hath over-reach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed the Seller, and got a great advantage to himself. This he notes as a common but reprovable practice.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 There is gold <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">To wit, in the World, in divers mens hands, by whom it is highly prized.</ns0:note>, and a multitude of rubies, but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 3. 15. & 8. 11.</ns0:note> the lips of knowledge <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> a precious jewel <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">But wise speeches proceeding from an under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing or honest Heart are of far greater worth and use, both to him that uttereth them<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and to those that receive and improve them to their own benefit.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 22. 27. & 27. 13.</ns0:note> Take his garment <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">To wit, as a Pledge, without which he ought not to be tru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sted, because by this action he sheweth himself to be a Fool, and he taketh the ready way to beggery. <ns0:hi>Obj.</ns0:hi> This precept contra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dicts that Law which forbad the taking of a Garment for a Pledge, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 22. 26. <ns0:hi>Answ..</ns0:hi> It doth not contradict it, for the cases vast<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly differ; for that Law concerned onely the Poor, who were forced to borrow for their own necessity, and therefore deserve pity; whereas this reacheth onely those who are or would be thought rich and sufficient Security for others, and who borrow not for their own need, but for a meer Stranger, for which folly they de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serve to be severely punished. Besides, this may be onely a Pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diction, though it be delivered in the form of a Precept, as many Predictions are; and so shews what may be expected by him that is guilty of such folly, even that he shall be stripped of his Garments and other necessaries.</ns0:note> that is surety <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> a stran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ger <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">For a Forreigner or a Person unknown to him.</ns0:note>, and take a pledg of him <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">That is surety: which words are to be understood out of the foregoing Clause.</ns0:note> for a strange wo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />man <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">For an Harlot, who is so called, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 2. 16. and elsewhere.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="18">18 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 15. 22.</ns0:note> Every purpose is established by counsel <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The way to bring our purposes and desires to a good effect, is to manage them with serious consideration and good advice.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>therefore.</ns0:hi> This is necessary in every common undertaking, and much more in a thing of such high importance as War is.</ns0:note>

                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> Candle.</ns0:note> lamp <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">His comfort and happiness, his Name and Memory which are oft compared in Scripture to a <ns0:hi>Lamp</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Light.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> shall be put out in obscure darkness <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Shall utterly perish; he shall die Childless, and with Ignominy.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 28. 20.</ns0:note> An inheritance may be gotten hastily at the be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ginning <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">An Estate somtimes is got suddenly in the very beginning of a Man's labours for it, in which case it may be presumed that some undirect and unrighteous courses were used, for the getting of it, because Riches are very seldom given by God, or gotten by men, without mens diligence. But this, as well as many other Proverbs, are to be understood of the common course, although it admit of some exceptions. For somtimes Merchants or others get great E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />states speedily by one happy Voyage, or by some other prosperous event. This Translation follows the Hebrew Marginal reading, but according to the Textual reading, it may be thus rendered and un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood, <ns0:hi>An Inheritance gotten in the beginning</ns0:hi> (to wit, of a mans in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deavours) <ns0:hi>is abominable,</ns0:hi> to wit, unto God, being supposed to be un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />justly gotten, as was now said.</ns0:note>, but the end thereof shall not be blessed <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">At last it shall be cursed and wither by God's just judgment.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="23">23 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Vers. 10.</ns0:note> Divers weights <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> an abomination unto the LORD <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Of which see above on <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 10.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> balan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces of deceit.</ns0:note> a false balance <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> not good <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Is very wicked and hateful to God and men.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 37. 23. Ch. 16. 9. Jer. 10. 23.</ns0:note> Man's goings <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">All mens purposes and actions.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> of the LORD <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Are ordered and over-ruled by God's wise and powerful Providence to accomplish his own counsel and good pleasure, and not what men list or intend</ns0:note>; how can a man then understand his own way <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Either 1. what course he ought to take; which he cannot know without God's direction and assistance, Compare <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 16. 9. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 10. 23. Or 2. what the issue of his designs will be, whether they shall succeed or be disappointed, <ns0:hi>the way</ns0:hi> being taken for the end or event to which it leads, as it is in many other places. The scope of the Proverb is to shew, that all the events of humane life are neither ordered nor foreseen by Mans, but onely by God's Providence, and therefore men should onely mind the doing of their duty, and then quietly depend upon God for a good Issue to their endeavours.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 <ns0:hi>It is</ns0:hi> a snare <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">It brings guilt and God's curse and vengeance upon him.</ns0:note> to the man <ns0:hi>who</ns0:hi> devoureth <ns0:hi>that which is</ns0:hi> holy <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Those Meats or Drinks which were devoted or consecrated to God. Under which one kind he comprehends and forbids all alienation of Sacred or Dedicated things from God to a Man's pri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vate use or benefit: Of which see <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 27. 9. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 23. 21. <ns0:hi>Mal.</ns0:hi> 3<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 8, 9. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 5. 1, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and after vows to make enquiry <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">After a Man hath made Vows to consider whether he can possibly, or may lawfully keep them, and to invent or enquire of others all ways possible to break his Vow, and to satisfie or deceive his Conscience in so doing. Which enquiry is justly cen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sured as a sin and snare, because it is an evidence of a covetous or irreligious Mind, and is the ready way and first step towards the open violation of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 101. 5, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> Vers. 3.</ns0:note> A wise king <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Who seriously minds his Duty and his true interest.</ns0:note> scattereth <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Breaks their Companies and Consederacies, and forceth them to flee se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veral ways for their own safety, driveth them from his presence, and from the Society of honest men, as the Chaff is by the Hus<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bandman separated from the Corn, and driven away by the Wind, of which this Hebrew word is commonly used; and to which the next Clause hath some reference.</ns0:note> the wicked and bringeth the wheel over them. <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>s</ns0:hi> As the Cart-wheel was an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciently turned over the Sheaves to beat the Corn out of them, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 28. 27, 28. He punisheth them severely, as their Offences de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serve. This or such like punishments were not unusual among the Eastern Nations, as we may gather from, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 8. 2. & 12. 31 <ns0:hi>Amos</ns0:hi> 1. 3.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:533" />27 The spirit <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The reasonable Soul.</ns0:note> of a man <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> lamp.</ns0:note> candle <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Is a clear and glorious light set up in Man for his information and direction.</ns0:note> of the LORD <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">So called partly because it comes from God in a more immediate and peculiar manner than the Body doth, <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 12. 7. and partly because it is in Gods stead to observe and judge all a Man's actions.</ns0:note>, searching all the inward parts of the belly <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Discern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing not onely his outward actions, which are visible to others, but his most inward and secret thoughts and affections, which no other Man can see, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2. 11. <ns0:hi>The Belly</ns0:hi> is here put for the Heart, as it is frequently. The Soul can reflect upon and judge of its own dispositions and actions. Which plainly sheweth that the Heart is not so deceitful, but that a Man by diligent study of it, and the use of the means appointed by God, may arrive at a certain know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge of its state and condition, in reference to God, and to Salva<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 101. 1.                   <ns0:p n="29">29 The glory of young men <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">That wherein they glory as their Priviledge above old men.</ns0:note>
